sens: A Levite in the service of King Jehoshaphat of Judah, tasked with teaching the Law in the cities of the kingdom
H2900G.detail: 1. Tobija is a Levite whom King Jehoshaphat sends to teach the Judeans the Law of the Lord. His name means "the Lord is good." He is part of a team of Levites and priests traveling through the cities of Judah to instruct the people. He is a man committed to the religious and educational work of God's people at a time when the kingdom was divided (2 Chronicles 17:8).
H2900G.origine: The name Tobija comes from two Hebrew roots: "Tob" which means "good" and "Yah" (an abbreviation of the divine name Jehovah). His name thus expresses a statement of faith: "Jehovah is good." It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing trust in the goodness of the Lord.
H2900G.emploi: Tobija is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 17:8. He is one of the Levites sent by King Jehoshaphat of Judah, around the 9th century B.C., for a teaching ministry. He represents those servants of God who, while not in the forefront of the biblical narrative, played a crucial role in the transmission of the Law and the instruction of the people of Israel.

sens: A family that returned from Babylonian exile
Descendants of Tobija unable to prove their Israelite origin
H2900H.detail:
1. Tobija is the name of a family mentioned in the lists of those who returned from Babylonian captivity with Zerubbabel. This family appears in Ezra 2:60 and Nehemiah 7:62, where it is listed among the families whose descent from Israel could not be established with certainty.
2. The sons of Tobija are included in the register of the returning exiles, but they could not justify their Israelite genealogy with documents or testimonies. This was a delicate situation: they were part of the group returning to rebuild the people, but their connection to Israel remained uncertain in the eyes of the religious authorities.
H2900H.origine: The name Tobija means "Jehovah is good" in Hebrew, composed of "Tov" (good) and the divine name Jah (Jehovah). It is a classic theophoric name that expresses trust in the goodness of the Lord. Several characters bore this name in the history of Israel, indicating that it was common among the people.
H2900H.emploi: Tobija is mentioned twice in the Bible, always in the records of the exiles returned from Babylon. In Ezra 2:60 and Nehemiah 7:62, the sons of Tobija are listed among a group of families whose authentic Israelite origin could not be affirmed. These two parallel passages come from the same official register compiled at the time of Zerubbabel and Ezra. The presence of this family in the list did not automatically exclude them from the return and reconstruction, but it raised a question of identity that concerned the leaders of the restored community.
H2900H.portee: This account reminds us that the return from exile was not a pure and unambiguous event, but raised practical and theological questions about the true identity of God's people. It invites reflection on the grace of God that welcomes those who turn to Him, even beyond genealogical or administrative questions.

sens: An Ammonite adversary who opposed the rebuilding of Jerusalem under Nehemiah
H2900I.detail: Tobija is a proper name referring to a prominent figure in the account of the rebuilding of Jerusalem during Nehemiah's time (c. 445 B.C.). Although he is referred to as a "servant of the Ammonites" (Nehemiah 2:10), he possesses considerable resources and influence: he maintains correspondence with the nobles of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 6:19), his family alliances connect him to the main defenders of the city (his son-in-law is Shecaniah, Nehemiah 6:18), and he even has a room in the temple itself (Nehemiah 13:7). Along with Sanballat the Horonite and Geshem the Arab, Tobija leads a systematic campaign against Nehemiah: he mocks the rebuilding project (Nehemiah 4:3), organizes a false invitation to lure him out of the city (Nehemiah 6:1-2), employs prophets to intimidate him (Nehemiah 6:14), and creates a network of propaganda to discredit him (Nehemiah 6:19).
H2900I.origine: The name Tobija means "Jehovah is good" (from Yah, an abbreviation of Yahweh, and the verb "to be good"). It is a typically Hebrew name, indicating that Tobija, although classified as an "Ammonite," had integrated into the culture and religion of Israel. Several characters bear this name in the Old Testament, but this one is primarily known for his role as an opponent to Nehemiah's project.
H2900I.emploi: Tobija appears 12 times in the book of Nehemiah, exclusively in chapters 2 to 13, which cover the period of the rebuilding of the walls and the religious reform. He is consistently associated with Sanballat and other enemies of the project. The text shows the escalation of his opposition: first he expresses his discontent (2:10), then he participates in mockery (4:3), next he conspires with others to thwart Nehemiah (6:1-2), and finally the high priest Eliashib gives him access to the temple (13:7), revealing the internal corruption that Nehemiah must combat. His story illustrates how opposition to God's project can come from both outside and inside.
H2900I.portee: The example of Tobija teaches the reader that the spiritual and physical rebuilding of God's people always encounters opposition, sometimes organized and cunning. His story also shows that this opposition can come from influential figures who combine social status with malice. For the believer, Tobija serves as a reminder of the importance of vigilance and dependence on God in the face of criticism and attempts to discourage, as illustrated by Nehemiah's prayer: "Remember, O my God, Tobija" (6:14).

sens: A man who brings gifts to the temple upon the return from exile
A man tasked with receiving the gifts of the captives returned from Babylon
H2900J.detail: 1. Tobija is a man living at the time of the return from exile (around 520 B.C.). His name means "the Lord is good." He appears in the book of Zechariah as one of the three individuals responsible for receiving the offerings from the exiles returned from Babylon (Zechariah 6:10). 2. Along with Heldaï and Jedaiah, Tobija goes to the house of Josiah, son of Zephaniah, to collect the precious gifts from the captives. These gifts will be used to make crowns for the temple of the Lord, in remembrance of this miraculous return (Zechariah 6:14).
H2900J.origine: The name Tobija is composed of two Hebrew roots: "tov" (good) and "yah" (an abbreviation of the divine name Yahweh). It literally means "the Lord is good" or "Yahweh is good." This type of theophoric name was common among the Israelites and expressed trust in the goodness of God. The form "Tobija" appears in the texts of the return from exile.
H2900J.emploi: Tobija is mentioned twice in the book of Zechariah, both in chapter 6, in the context of the rebuilding of the temple after the Babylonian exile (Zechariah 6:10 and 6:14). He is part of the characters who embody the hope and restoration of Israel. His role is to receive the voluntary contributions of the exiles returned from Babylon, symbolizing the community's commitment to the reconstruction of religious and communal life. These verses place Tobija at a key moment in biblical history: the renewal of the people and worship after seventy years of captivity.
H2900J.portee: The account of Tobija reminds us that the return from exile was not just a political liberation, but also a spiritual renewal. His participation in the collection of offerings shows how everyone was invited to contribute to the rebuilding of the temple and the restoration of the worship of the Lord. This story encourages the modern reader to recognize that God remains good to His people, even after the greatest trials, and to actively engage in communal and spiritual life.

sens: Transform fibers into thread by twisting them together
Work the thread by hand to make it a weaveable material
H2901.detail:
1. To spin means to twist together fibers — flax, wool, hair — to make continuous thread. It is a manual and patient task, accomplished by pulling the fibers with one hand while twisting them with the other. In the days of the desert, the women of Israel spun goat hair to create the material that would be used for the curtains of the Tabernacle (Exodus 35:26).
2. By extension, spinning refers to the entire process of transforming raw materials into threads ready to be woven. This work required skill and know-how: the Bible notes that the women who spun had skill (Exodus 35:25), a personal gift and experience.
H2901.origine: The Hebrew verb tavah comes from the root tav, which evokes the action of twisting, turning. The image is that of the spinner who continuously turns their fingers or spindle to transform raw fiber into a regular and strong thread. The same root appears in other words of the Hebrew language that describe actions of twisting or turning.
H2901.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the context of the construction of the Tabernacle in the desert (Exodus 35). The women of Israel, endowed with skill and a willing heart, spun dyed linen in precious colors (blue, purple, crimson) and goat hair. These spun threads were not merely a domestic craft: they were part of the composition of the sacred fabrics of the sanctuary. The word emphasizes both the technical skill required and the voluntary and generous contribution of the women to the work of God.
H2901.portee: This word shows us that God welcomes tangible talents and manual skills as an offering to His service. The women who spun were not high priestesses, but they patiently transformed raw materials into precious threads for the Tabernacle. It is a lesson for every believer: ordinary work, done wholeheartedly, becomes a contribution to the glory of God.

sens: apply a coating, a protective layer on a surface
plaster or mortar the walls of a house
cover with a precious material to beautify or protect
hide, conceal under an appearance of solidity
H2902A.detail: 1. The primary concrete meaning is to apply a layer of material on a surface intended to protect or adorn. Leviticus 14:42-43 speaks of recoating a house afflicted with leprosy: the contaminated stones are removed, and then new mortar is applied to restore the wall. In 1 Chronicles 29:4, it refers to covering the interior walls of a building with gold and silver: the same action of covering, but with precious materials. 2. The word is particularly used for plaster or mortar applied to walls. This is suggested in Ezekiel 13:10-11, where the false prophets cover the walls with plaster — in other words, they apply a superficial layer without repairing the fragility of the inner wall. 3. Figuratively, the image of plaster hiding underlying decay expresses deception: pretending that all is well (“Peace! when there is no peace”) while masking a destructive reality.
H2902A.origine: The Hebrew root טוח (tûah) denotes the action of stretching, extending a material over a surface to cover it. The verb can be used with or without a direct object: one can recoat (a house, a wall) or simply cover. This action is always visible; it transforms the outward appearance of what it covers.
H2902A.emploi: The verb appears ten times in the Old Testament, mainly in the laws of purity in Leviticus (law on leprosy of houses) and in the oracles of Ezekiel against false prophets. In Leviticus 14, recoating is an act of restoration and purification: it is an objective step in the process of healing and declaring purity. In Ezekiel 13, the same verb takes on a critical value: recoating becomes the image of the dishonesty of prophets who hide moral and spiritual collapse under reassuring words. The context completely changes the meaning: the same gesture is sometimes necessary, sometimes condemnable.
H2902A.portee: This word invites the reader to distinguish appearance from reality. A recoated wall can be perfectly healthy — this is legitimate and necessary. But it can also hide a deep crack that the plaster temporarily masks. For the Christian, it is a call to sincerity: not to settle for repairing what is visible, but to heal what rots in secret. The false prophets of Ezekiel show the danger of preaching peace when there is spiritual decay: plaster never saves.

sens: Have a closed mind, unable to understand
Be mentally blinded, as if coated with a substance that covers and obstructs
H2902B.detail:
1. The word evokes the image of a surface covered, coated, blocked — as if something had been "spread" over the eyes or mind to prevent it from functioning. In Isaiah 44:18, the idolaters have "closed understanding," unable to see the absurdity of their worship of wooden statues: they are spiritually blind and deaf to reason.
2. It is a moral and spiritual incapacity, not mere ignorance: one who has such a closed understanding cannot comprehend, even if they wanted to, because a hostile force (here, divine judgment) has taken away their ability. The text states that God "has closed their eyes" and "their heart."
H2902B.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the action of covering, coating, smearing a surface. The basic image is very concrete: something that "spreads" or "covers" the organ of thought, like a substance that obstructs sight or judgment. It is from this tangible image that the spiritual meaning arises.
H2902B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 44:18. It is a text where the prophet denounces the absurdity of idolatry: those who make and worship idols cannot understand their folly because God "has closed their eyes and their heart." The word emphasizes that this is not mere ignorance, but a true spiritual closure — a hardening of the heart and mind.
H2902B.portee: This word reminds us of a serious truth: the voluntary refusal to acknowledge God can lead to a hardening of the mind, where one becomes incapable of understanding what is evident. It is a warning against the worship of false gods — including modern idols — and an invitation to keep the heart open to the word of God as long as one still can.

sens: Band or ornament worn on the forehead, between the eyes
Visible mark of a commitment or covenant with God
Sign reminding of obedience to the word of the Lord
H2903.detail:
1. A frontlet is a band, a kind of ribbon worn on the forehead, between the eyes. The word evokes a visible insignia, a bodily mark. This is what God commands: "It shall be as a sign on your hand and as frontlets between your eyes" (Exodus 13:16).

2. Spiritually, the frontlet symbolizes a visible link with the divine covenant, the commitment of the heart to God's commandments. It is a permanent reminder: "You shall bind them as a sign on your hands, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes" (Deuteronomy 6:8).

3. The frontlet expresses the idea that the word of God must be constantly present in thought and guide action. By wearing it, one proclaims: "I remember the Lord and obey His word" (Deuteronomy 11:18).
H2903.origine: The Hebrew word *tophaphah* derives from a root meaning "to wrap" or "to bind." It literally describes what wraps around or attaches. In post-biblical Jewish liturgy, this symbolic image of frontlets became phylacteries — small boxes containing verses of the Law that devout Jews actually wore on their foreheads and arms. However, in the Hebrew Bible, the word primarily retains its meaning of "sign" or "mark" worn, whether physical or mental.
H2903.emploi: The word frontlet appears only three times in the Bible, all in the passages from Exodus and Deuteronomy related to the commandments: Exodus 13:16, Deuteronomy 6:8, and Deuteronomy 11:18. Each time, it concerns memorizing the words of the Lord and the covenant of salvation, particularly the exodus from Egypt. The image is one of personal commitment, a mark that the believer bears to testify to their covenant with God and to constantly remember their duty of obedience. It is primarily figurative language: the word of God must be "bound" to the hand (action) and between the eyes (thought).
H2903.portee: For the believer, the frontlet reminds that the word of God is not an abstract doctrine, but a concrete commitment that must govern both thought and action. Wearing the Law "between the eyes" means not losing sight of it, keeping it at the center of consciousness. It is an exhortation to make one's faith visible through actions and to deeply root the promises and commandments of the Lord in one's heart.

sens: To throw something with force
To overturn, knock someone down
To chase away, expel
To direct towards a place
To make fall, set in motion
To carry, transport from one place to another
H2904.detail:
1. To throw something with force: it is to project an object into the air or towards a place. Saul "throws" his spear at David (1 Samuel 18:11). The lot is "thrown" into a garment to know the will of God (Proverbs 16:33).
2. To overturn, knock someone down: it is to bring down or subjugate, to put to the ground. Job asks if the mere sight of Leviathan does not "overturn" the one who sees it (Job 40:28).
3. To chase away, expel: it is to forcefully make someone leave, to reject. Jeconiah and his descendants are "thrown" out of their land (Jeremiah 22:28).
4. To direct towards a place: it is to send or make go. God "directs" His fury (Isaiah 22:17).
5. To make fall, set in motion: it is to create a movement that brings down or destroys. God "makes a mighty wind blow" on the sea, which triggers the storm (Jonah 1:4).
6. To carry, transport from one place to another: it is to move, to exile. God promises to "carry" His people to a land they do not know (Jeremiah 16:13).
H2904.origine: The verb טוּל comes from a root that evokes the action of projecting or throwing. In Hebrew, this root is linked to the idea of violent movement and forced displacement. The word has several verbal forms (Pilpel, Hiphil, Hophal) that nuance the action: the most intensive (Pilpel) emphasizes the violence of the gesture, the Hiphil form makes it an action directed by an agent, and the Hophal form describes the person or thing affected by the action.
H2904.emploi: This verb appears 14 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly among the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Jonah) and in the Psalms and Proverbs. It describes various actions: throwing a spear (1 Samuel 18:11), casting lots (Proverbs 16:33), overturning by fear (Job 40:28), exiling a people (Jeremiah 16:13, 22:28), or triggering a storm (Jonah 1:4). Often, the context highlights power, judgment, or authority: whether it is a weapon thrown by a king, an exile ordered by God, or a storm sent by the Lord. In the narratives of Jonah, the same verb describes both the wind that God "makes blow" and the decision to throw Jonah overboard.
H2904.portee: This word reveals the power of God acting unimpeded: He can overturn, exile, destroy. But it also shows that every event — even what seems chaotic or violent — is under His hand. For the believer, it is a call to recognize God's sovereignty, even in difficult circumstances, and not to believe in chance: "Every decision comes from the Lord" (Proverbs 16:33).

sens: Line of elements arranged side by side or one after another
Set of precious stones aligned
Series of columns or beams in a building
Level or floor of a construction
H2905.detail:
1. The primary meaning is a sequence of objects placed in line, in a regular order. It is a row in the sense we know: things side by side. The precious stones of the high priest's breastplate are arranged as follows: "four rows of stones" (Exodus 28:17), each row containing four different stones aligned horizontally.
2. In constructions, this word specifically refers to rows of stones or beams: the house of the forest of Lebanon "rested on four rows of cedar columns" (1 Kings 7:2), meaning four lines of columns arranged parallel that supported the building.
3. The word can also describe a floor or level of vertical construction, since a "row" of beams forms a horizontal plane of the building. This is why the Segond sometimes translates this word as "floor."
4. Finally, there can be several rows in a circle or around the perimeter of an object: "gourds, arranged in two rows" around a large basin (1 Kings 7:24), forming a symmetrical decoration.
H2905.origine: The Hebrew word tur comes from a root that evokes the idea of "turn" or "course" — the sense of moving in line. It expresses the action of aligning things. This root also appears in other Hebrew words of the same family that retain this notion of ordered succession or circuit.
H2905.emploi: The word appears about twenty times in the Bible, mainly in the detailed descriptions of the tabernacle and its ornaments (Exodus 28, 39) and in the grand construction projects of King Solomon (1 Kings 6 and 7, and 2 Chronicles 4). It also appears in the prophetic vision of Ezekiel concerning the future temple (Ezekiel 46:23). It is a very concrete and architectural word: the Bible uses it when it wants to give the reader a precise and orderly image of what it describes — stones arranged in order, columns aligned according to a plan. The text does not give it any figurative or spiritual meaning; it is always a material description.
H2905.portee: This word reminds the reader that God loves order, harmony, and beauty. The tabernacle and Solomon's constructions are not improvisations, but carefully thought-out edifices, where each element has its place. By reading how God gives instructions for these rows of precious stones and columns, the believer sees that God does not ask for raw beauty, but for organized, symmetrical, thoughtful beauty. It is a silent teaching about the seriousness with which God wants to be worshiped.

sens: A mass of earth that rises high above the surrounding ground
Power or force that dominates and fills everything
H2906.detail:
1. A mountain is a large elevation of land, an imposing rocky mass: in King Nebuchadnezzar's dream, a stone is cut out from a mountain without human intervention (Daniel 2:45), suggesting a sovereign divine action.
2. Figuratively, the mountain becomes a symbol of power and permanent domination: the stone that strikes the statue becomes a great mountain that fills the whole earth (Daniel 2:35), representing God's eternal kingdom that engulfs all human kingdoms and persists forever.
H2906.origine: The Aramaic word tur comes from the same root as the Hebrew word tsur (צוּר), which means "rock" or "cliff." This root first evokes the solid and unchanging stone, then expands to the entire mountain—the image of something massive, stable, and permanent. In the Old Testament, the mountain is often the place where God manifests or establishes His power.
H2906.emploi: The Aramaic word tur appears only twice in the Bible, both in chapter 2 of Daniel, which reports the interpretation of King Nebuchadnezzar's prophetic dream. In this context, the mountain is not just a geographical feature, but a prophetic image of the universal and lasting dominion of God's kingdom. The fact that it forms from a stone that is cut out "without the help of any hand" emphasizes that this power comes from God alone, not from human effort.
H2906.portee: This word invites the reader to understand that God's kingdom is not established by political or military force, but by God's direct and sovereign intervention. The mountain that fills the whole earth speaks of God's final and definitive victory: a promise of assurance for the believer living under ephemeral human kingdoms.

sens: to rush quickly and forcefully upon a prey
to move rapidly and impetuously
H2907.detail:
1. To rush quickly and forcefully upon a prey — this is the image of a bird of prey suddenly descending from the sky to seize its victim. The verb evokes this violent and decisive movement. In Job 9:26, the eagle that "swoops" on its prey illustrates this sudden and irresistible attack, just as the days flee quickly.
2. To move rapidly and impetuously — more broadly, the word expresses any movement that combines speed, force, and suddenness, without necessarily implying predation. It is a striking contrast to slowness: the days pass like the rushes that "swoop" on the water.
H2907.origine: The Hebrew verb טוּשׂ comes from a root that evokes rapid and violent movement. The context of Job 9:26 associates it with the traditional image of the eagle descending on its prey, a classic biblical motif of power and swiftness.
H2907.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible. In Job 9:26, Job uses it to compare the fleeting of his days to the action of the eagle swooping down on its prey. The context is one of lament: Job compares the flow of time to irresistible and rapid movements, highlighting human helplessness in the face of life's speed.
H2907.portee: This word reminds us of the passage of time that flows without return and the power of forces that escape us. For Job, as for us, the image of the eagle swooping is one of certainty — that of death approaching inevitably. It invites reflection on the brevity of life and the wisdom of using it well.

sens: the state of one who abstains from eating
the manner of voluntarily depriving oneself of food
H2908.detail: 1. Fasting is the act of not eating, either out of necessity or by voluntary choice. In Daniel 6:18, King Darius spends the night "fasting": he does not take a meal, likely troubled by his concern for Daniel thrown into the lion's den. It is a physical state and a sign of inner turmoil. 2. Fasting can also express a voluntary deprivation, often linked to prayer, penitence, or deep mourning. Although this text is unique in the Hebrew Bible, fasting is elsewhere associated with humility before God and the sincerity of supplication.
H2908.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be hungry" or "to have hunger." It describes the state of one who deprives themselves of food. The context of Daniel 6:18 shows a fast resulting from anxiety rather than a deliberate religious practice, although both senses are close: the absence of food accompanies a troubled state of the soul.
H2908.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 6:18. King Darius, after ordering that Daniel be thrown to the lions for his faithfulness to God, spends the night troubled: he does not eat, does not entertain himself with his concubines, and does not find sleep. His involuntary fast reflects his moral agitation. Elsewhere in the Bible, fasting is often a voluntary religious act, but here it is the expression of a troubled conscience.
H2908.portee: This passage shows that fasting can be the result of sincere worry or compassion. King Darius, though pagan, feels a deep enough guilt to lose his appetite and sleep: it is an indication that the heart can be touched by the fate of a righteous man. For the believer, this account reminds us that our attitude toward God's servants does not leave us indifferent.

sens: The distance an arrow can travel when shot from a bow
By extension, a short or moderate distance
H2909.detail:
1. The range of an arrow is literally the distance to which an arrow launched from a bow can fly. It is a practical and ancient measure: it designates the space an archer can cover with their shot. In Genesis 21:16, Hagar sits far from her son Ishmael, at "a range of an arrow" — that is, at a very precise distance, far enough not to see his agony, but close enough to keep him in mind.
2. By extension, the word is used to denote a measurable and moderate distance, not immediate proximity nor a very great distance, but a separation that can be controlled by sight or sound.
H2909.origine: The Hebrew verb טָחָה (tachah) fundamentally means "to throw" or "to project," as one propels an arrow. It belongs to the vocabulary of archery and ranged combat. Here, the passive particle forms a nominal expression: "that which is shot" or "that which is reached by shooting," hence "range of shot." The image is military and concrete, rooted in the reality of ancient archery.
H2909.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 21:16. Hagar, sent away by Abraham into the desert with her dying son Ishmael, distances herself from him so as not to see his death. She sits precisely "at a range of an arrow" — far enough to respect an intolerable pain, but close enough to remain aware of his fate. It is a measure of both love and distress: she wants to spare her heart the fatal moment while keeping the connection.
H2909.portee: This touching detail shows how the Bible honors the concrete words of pain. Hagar does not abandon Ishmael — she takes a precise distance, neither fleeing nor abandoning. It is a lesson on the weight of suffering and the limits of what one can bear: there are thresholds, spaces where love breathes when it can no longer act.

sens: The seat of deep thoughts and feelings, the innermost part of being
What is hidden or secret within oneself, away from the gaze of others
The center, what is deepest
H2910.detail: 1. The word designates the inner seat of thoughts and feelings: it is where consciousness, reflection, and intention reside. In Job 38:36, God asks, "Who has put wisdom in the heart?" referring to the seat of judgment and intelligence. 2. It evokes what is secret, hidden within — what does not appear on the outside. In Psalms 51:8, the psalmist asks God for "truth in the innermost being," meaning deep sincerity, not a hypocritical appearance. 3. It is also the very center, what is at the heart of a person, the core of their spiritual being.
H2910.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to enclose," "to cover." It literally designates the "inner regions" or "hidden parts." It is not the physical heart (organ), but the heart as the seat of emotions, will, and conscience — the heart understood in a Semitic way, the center of the whole being.
H2910.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Job 38:36, it refers to the seat of wisdom and intelligence: God asks who has endowed creatures with inner wisdom. In Psalms 51:8, in King David's prayer of repentance, it designates the deep desire for truth within oneself, the sincerity of heart that God demands. Both usages speak of an inner reality: wisdom in Job, truth in the psalmist.
H2910.portee: This word invites the believer not to settle for outward obedience: God looks at the heart, at hidden thoughts and intentions. It reminds us that true fear of God and spiritual truth must be rooted not on the surface, but deep within our being. It is a call to authenticity before God.

sens: cylindrical stone used to grind grains
the action or work of grinding
a burdensome or oppressive task
H2911.detail:
1. A millstone is a round, flat stone, or two stacked stones, that is operated to grind grain into flour. It is a very ancient and common tool in households (Lamentations 5:13).
2. The word also designates the act of grinding itself, the daily and repetitive work of transforming grain.
3. Because this work is hard, monotonous, and requires great physical strength (especially for young people as shown in Lamentations 5:13), the millstone symbolizes an overwhelming labor, an endless chore.
H2911.origine: The Hebrew word טְחוֹן (techon) comes from a root meaning "to grind" or "to reduce to powder." The millstone is the quintessential instrument of domestic grinding, known since prehistoric times in the Mediterranean. It is such a familiar object in daily life that its name immediately evokes hard labor.
H2911.emploi: The word appears only once in the Old Testament, in Lamentations 5:13, in the heart of a lament about the suffering of the people after the destruction of Jerusalem. The prophet enumerates the humiliations inflicted on young men: they had to perform the chore of grinding grain at the millstone, a hard and degrading task imposed on captives by the occupier. The millstone here represents not only an exhausting physical task but also enslavement and loss of dignity.
H2911.portee: This word reminds believers that God sees the sufferings and humiliations of His people, even the most mundane and forgotten. It invites us to have compassion for those who endure overwhelming work or injustice, and to recognize that God does not turn a blind eye to these realities.

sens: To reduce grain or a substance to fine powder with a millstone
To crush, grind a solid substance until it becomes impalpable
Figuratively, to oppress or overwhelm someone
H2912.detail: 1. The most common meaning is that of daily work: grinding grain between two millstones to make flour. This is what women do in Ecclesiastes 12:5 ("those who grind cease because they are diminished") — a task so usual that it symbolizes ordinary life, and its cessation signals old age and weakness. 2. The verb also applies to substances other than grain: Moses grinds the golden calf until it is reduced to fine powder (Deuteronomy 9:21), or the Israelites grind the manna with millstones (Numbers 11:8). The idea is always one of complete, methodical reduction to fine particles. 3. Figuratively, the verb expresses oppression and crushing: in Isaiah 3:15, the Lord accuses the leaders of trampling and "crushing the faces of the poor." To grind someone's face or crush someone is to subdue them, to grind them under one's weight.
H2912.origine: The Hebrew verb טָחַן (ta.chan) comes from a root expressing the action of grinding, of reducing to crumbs. Its basic image is mechanical and concrete: it is the action of the mill, the friction between the two stones. The same root produces nominal forms to designate the millstone itself. The verb is well attested in biblical and rabbinic Hebrew for all uses of grinding.
H2912.emploi: The verb appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in domestic or narrative contexts. It first describes the work of women: grinding grain is a common task (Ecclesiastes 12:5, alluding to Job 31:10), and a form of slavery after capture (Judges 16:21: Samson condemned to turn the millstone in prison). It also appears in dramatic narratives: the destruction of the golden calf (Deuteronomy 9:21) and the treatment of the manna (Numbers 11:8). In Isaiah, the verb shifts to the figurative sense of oppression (Isaiah 3:15). The word is also found in the ironic context of Isaiah 47:2, where Babylon is invited to grind like a slave.
H2912.portee: This word roots the Christian in the reality of human labor and vulnerability. The millstone symbolizes daily, necessary, and humble work; its cessation signals the fragility of life. Above all, the shift from the concrete sense to the figurative sense (crushing the poor) reminds us that power can become oppression: it is a call to justice and respect for those who cannot defend themselves.

sens: round, flat stone used to grind grains
figuratively, an instrument of daily and mundane work
H2913.detail:
1. A millstone is a round, flat stone used to crush wheat or barley grains and turn them into flour. It is a common household tool in the ancient world, often used by women. In Ecclesiastes 12:6, the millstone represents that familiar sound of daily life that weakens — an image of life slowing down and vigor declining with age.
2. Figuratively, the millstone represents daily work, the ordinary tasks of life. Its regular operation symbolizes routine and normalcy; when its noise ceases or weakens, it is a sign that something essential is changing — here, the approach of death and the end of strength.
H2913.origine: The Hebrew word טַחֲנָה (ta.cha.nah) comes from the root טחן (ta.chan), which means "to grind" or "to crush." This root expresses the action of reducing to powder, paste, or flour by rubbing or crushing between two surfaces. The millstone itself is the instrument that performs this action — the object that bears the name of the verb that characterizes it.
H2913.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ecclesiastes 12:6. It is found in a poetic description of human aging, where the wise man enumerates the signs of physical decline: the millstone that weakens symbolizes here the gradual extinguishing of vital forces. It is a passage that is both concrete and highly symbolic, where each image — the silver chain, the golden cord, the pitcher, the wheel — describes the loosening of the ties that keep us alive.
H2913.portee: This image of the millstone that weakens invites the reader to meditate on the fragility of life and the inevitability of aging. It calls for wisdom: to live consciously of the time given, to recognize that our strengths are limited and temporary, and to prepare to accept what we cannot control. It is a subtle yet profound invitation to place our trust beyond earthly things.

sens: Painful and bleeding swelling at the anus or rectum
Tumor or growth on the body
Wound, affliction sent by God as punishment
H2914.detail:
1. An hemorrhoid is a swelling of the blood vessels at the lower rectum, causing pain and bleeding: this is the literal and medical sense of the word. In Deuteronomy 28:27, the Lord threatens Israel with hemorrhoids among other diseases.
2. The word more broadly refers to any tumor or fleshy growth on the body, not just in the lower abdomen. In the account of the Philistines (1 Samuel 5-6), after the Ark of God entered their land, hemorrhoids struck the inhabitants "from the least to the greatest" (1 Samuel 5:9), and they made "figures of your tumors" in gold to offer as restitution (1 Samuel 6:4-5).
3. In the biblical context, hemorrhoids become a supernatural plague, a mark of divine intervention against a people who have sinned. They are not merely a natural misfortune, but an affliction sent by God as judgment, as a sign to be recognized and rectified.
H2914.origine: The Hebrew word טְחֹר (téhor) literally denotes a growth or tumor. Its etymology suggests the idea of swelling or inflammation. It belongs to a semantic field of skin diseases and bodily afflictions that, in ancient Israel, often signified the wrath of God. The account in 1 Samuel 5-6 makes it the visible sign of the power of the God of Israel over the Philistines.
H2914.emploi: The word appears 8 times, almost exclusively in 1 Samuel 5-6, during the account of the Ark of God among the Philistines. It also appears in Deuteronomy 28:27 in the list of the curses of the Covenant. All uses denote a bodily affliction: sometimes the Hebrew word is translated as "hemorrhoid" (when the plague affects the Philistines or threatens Israel), sometimes as "tumor" (when it refers to the golden figures that the Philistines make to seek forgiveness). The usage is concentrated and narrative: it is not a disease discussed in general, but a specific plague through which God manifests His fearsome presence.
H2914.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, illness is never neutral: it can be a sign of God's judgment, visibly striking one who has violated His order or profaned His honor. But it also shows that this affliction can be lifted and forgiven if one recognizes it and makes restitution — the Philistines, by offering a restitution of gold and confessing the power of the God of Israel, are delivered. It is an invitation to seek in suffering the finger of God and to respond with humility.

sens: coating or layer applied to a surface for protection or decoration
white coating used to whiten walls
H2915.detail:
1. Plaster is a layer of material (often white or lime) that is applied to a wall or structure to cover, protect, or beautify it. In the passage from Ezekiel 13:12, false prophets covered a wall with plaster without repairing its cracks: when the wall collapses, their superficial work collapses with it. This is the image of a repair that does not hold, a layer of paint on rotting wood.
2. Plaster also evokes the white coating that whitens tombs or buildings, giving an appearance of solidity and purity without guaranteeing the quality or durability of what is underneath. This is why Jesus later compares the scribes to "whited sepulchers."
H2915.origine: The Hebrew word טִיחַ (tiach) comes from a root meaning "to coat" or "to cover with a layer." It is a concrete word, derived from the language of construction and ancient building, where plaster and lime were the main materials for finishing walls. The underlying verb would evoke the action of "applying a coating" to a surface.
H2915.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 13:12. The prophet Ezekiel uses it to criticize the false prophets who prophesied peace in Jerusalem while disaster was approaching: they "daubed" the wall with plaster, that is, gave an illusion of safety without addressing the real problems. This image of superficial and fragile plaster symbolizes self-deception and words that do not hold up under trial.
H2915.portee: This word teaches the danger of relying on appearances or reassuring words that are not based on anything solid. For the believer, it reminds us that true solidity comes from an authentic relationship with God, not from a mere outer coating of piety. The collapsing plaster is a warning against prophets or teachers who preach lies.

sens: Soft and wet substance formed from soaked earth
Deposit or sediment at the bottom of murky water
Malleable material used to shape objects
Image of sin, filth, or a miserable situation
H2916.detail: 1. Mud is earth soaked with water, soft and sticky. It soils whoever treads on it: in 2 Samuel 22:43, the psalmist crushes his enemies "like the mud of the streets," an image of total destruction and humiliation. 2. Mud can also be a sludge, a muddy deposit that forms at the bottom of turbulent waters: in Isaiah 57:20, the sea of the wicked "raises the mire and the mud," evoking constant turmoil and impurity. 3. As raw material, mud or clay is what is shaped: it speaks of malleability and transformation, although the usages here emphasize the negative. 4. Spiritually, mud expresses a disastrous and shameful condition: in Psalms 69:15, the psalmist cries, "Deliver me from the mud," seeking salvation from sin and humiliation, while in Micah 7:10, the enemy will be "trampled underfoot like the mud of the streets," a symbol of divine judgment.
H2916.origine: The Hebrew word tit literally denotes mud or soft clay. It comes from a root that evokes moisture and malleability. In Aramaic, the related word tin (H2917) has the same meaning. This material, found everywhere in the Holy Land especially after rain or near waterways, was well known: mud from unpaved streets, potter's clay, silt from rivers. The word expresses the idea of formless substance, of filth, and by extension of baseness and distress.
H2916.emploi: The word appears 12 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms and the prophets. It first concretely denotes the mud of the paths: it is trampled underfoot (2 Samuel 22:43; Psalms 18:43; Micah 7:10). It can evoke muddy sludge: Isaiah 57:20 speaks of "waters" that "raise the mire and the mud." In Jeremiah 38:6 and Psalms 69:15, mud becomes an image of misfortune and peril, from which one must be rescued. In Zechariah 9:3, gold is compared to the "mud of the streets" to signify that its accumulated wealth is ultimately worthless. The context varies between humiliation, danger, and judgment of enemies.
H2916.portee: For the reader, mud speaks of spiritual degradation and peril. Crying out "Deliver me from the mud" (Psalms 69:15) expresses the distress of the heart that knows it is stuck in sin and calls for God's help. The image of trampling the mud underfoot reminds us that God's judgment crushes evil. Thus, mud becomes a language of authentic prayer and trust in divine power.

sens: Earthy material, soft and plastic, used to make pottery or bricks
Ordinary clay, symbol of fragility and materiality
H2917.detail: 1. Clay is the earth that potters shape to make vases and objects — it is a soft and malleable material before being hardened in fire. In Nebuchadnezzar's vision in Daniel 2, the feet of the statue are partly made of potter's clay and partly of iron: this clay represents a fragile and easily breakable material, unlike iron which is solid and durable. 2. Figuratively, clay symbolizes what is weak, fragile, and transient. When the prophet explains that iron does not mix with clay (Daniel 2:43), it means that two elements of such different natures cannot form a stable whole: clay crumbles while iron remains strong, just as kingdoms of unequal power cannot truly unite, even through marriages and alliances.
H2917.origine: The Aramaic word tin comes from the comparable Hebrew word טִיט (tit), which literally means "mud" or "slime." These two words describe the concrete image of wet, soft, and moldable earth — the raw material of the potter. It is a common word in ancient Near Eastern texts to designate this fundamental material of ceramics and construction.
H2917.emploi: The word appears twice in the Bible, in the two verses of the vision of the feet and toes of Nebuchadnezzar's statue (Daniel 2:41 and 2:43). In the first occurrence, clay is a constituent material of the statue's foot, mixed with iron. In the second, the prophet emphasizes the incompatibility of iron and clay: one is hard and indestructible, the other is brittle and fragile. This mixture in the feet of the statue symbolizes the instability of an empire or a future period that lacks internal unity.
H2917.portee: This image of clay reminds us that human powers, even imposing in appearance, rest on fragile foundations. By contemplating the contrast between iron and clay, the reader understands that only what is stable and united can truly endure, while what mixes incompatible or contradictory elements carries within it the seed of its own dissolution.

sens: Camp or set of tents set up temporarily
Group of fortified or delineated dwellings, especially for nomads or tribes
Rampart, fortification, or parapet of a city
Row or alignment of stones
Dwelling or place of residence
H2918.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a camp: a set of tents temporarily set up by nomads. This is the idea conveyed in Genesis 25:16 when it lists "the sons of Ishmael according to their enclosures" — the twelve tribal groups of Ishmael, each with its own camp.
2. The word also designates the structured set of dwellings of a group or tribe, fortified or well-defined. In 1 Chronicles 6:54, we see the "enclosures" assigned to the sons of Aaron: these are no longer tents, but cities or districts that belong to them.
3. In an urban context, the word can mean the parapets or battlements of a wall. In Song of Solomon 8:9, "silver battlements" adorn a fortified wall — it is the image of a citadel beautifully defended.
4. By extension, the word can refer to a simple row or alignment of stones, like an ordered structure.
5. More broadly, it means dwelling or habitation, the place where one resides. In Psalms 69:26, the psalmist wishes that the "dwelling" of his enemies be devastated.
H2918.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of arranging, ordering, or forming an enclosure. The basic image is that of a delimited structure, whether it be a camp of aligned tents or a fortified area. The same root appears in other Hebrew words meaning "row" or "order" — which explains why the term applies to both organized nomadic camps and structured cities.
H2918.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the Old Testament, mainly in geographical or administrative contexts. In Genesis and Ezekiel, it describes the settlements of tribes or foreign peoples (Ishmaelites, eastern peoples): these are organized groupings of dwellings. In 1 Chronicles, it applies to the allocation of cities to the sons of Aaron according to their clans and their "enclosures." In Psalms, it takes on the more general meaning of "dwelling" or habitation. In Song of Solomon, it spiritualizes by speaking of the battlements of a fortification, an image of the solid and beautiful character of a young woman. The word thus oscillates between the concrete idea of an organized camp and the broader idea of dwelling or defensive structure.
H2918.portee: This word helps the reader understand how ancient Israel thought about space and the organization of peoples: in terms of family or tribal groupings, each with its assigned territory. For the believer, it reminds us that God orders and limits the dwellings of peoples (Acts 17:26), and that He assigns each its place. The image of the fortified battlement also invites us to see the solidity and beauty of those established by God.

sens: Water droplets that form at night on plants and soil
Light moisture that nourishes and refreshes
Sign of divine blessing and life
What is fleeting and disappears quickly
Sweetness or sovereign favor of an authority
H2919.detail:
1. Dew is the water that condenses during the night and covers grass, plants, and soil in the early morning. In the Promised Land, where rains are scarce in summer, dew was essential for nourishing crops. Gideon performs a miraculous test by asking God for dew to cover the ground while his fleece remains dry (Judges 6:39).
2. This gentle and beneficial moisture symbolizes what sustains and gives life. The psalmist compares the dew descending on Mount Zion to the blessing that unites brothers in harmony (Psalms 133:3), and Job sees his roots nourished and the dew resting on his branches (Job 29:19).
3. Dew represents divine blessing and grace. When God blesses Jacob, He promises "the dew of heaven" along with fertility (Genesis 27:28). The words of the wise fall like dew that refreshes the greenery (Deuteronomy 32:2).
4. Conversely, dew evokes what evaporates and disappears: Hosea compares unfaithful Israel to dew that quickly dissipates (Hosea 13:3), showing the fragility of those who abandon God.
5. The favor of a king, sovereign and beneficial, is compared to dew on the grass (Proverbs 19:12), as it falls uncontrollably and refreshes like a shower.
H2919.origine: The Hebrew word tal literally means "that which falls lightly." It refers to the sensation of tiny, imperceptible droplets, but present. In Aramaic, the identical word tal (טַל) also designates dew. This simple term is rooted in the daily experience of Mediterranean and Palestinian nature, where nighttime dew was a regular and vital phenomenon for agriculture.
H2919.emploi: The word appears about 30 times in the Old Testament, especially in poetic and prophetic books (Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Hosea, Micah, Zechariah) and in the Torah. Literally, it denotes the meteorological phenomenon (Judges 6:37-40, Exodus 16:13-14). Spiritually, it symbolizes the divine blessing that falls gently (Genesis 27:28, Psalms 133:3), the prophetic word that nourishes (Deuteronomy 32:2), or conversely the ephemerality of what lacks substance (Hosea 13:3, 6:4). The context determines whether dew evokes grace, favor, or fragility.
H2919.portee: Dew reminds the believer that God's blessing, often discreet and imperceptible, is nonetheless daily and vital. It also teaches vigilance: what nourishes can also disappear, inviting everyone not to neglect the Eternal. This humble word enriches prayer and meditation by showing how God provides for the needs of the simplest and most hidden.

sens: Fine droplets of water that form at night on plants and soil
Humidity or fine rain falling from the sky
Liquid or substance soaking the body or clothing
H2920.detail:
1. Dew is the fine moisture that covers grass and plants when morning arrives, formed by the condensation of the night air. It is a common biblical image of freshness and life. In King Nebuchadnezzar's dream, the prophetic tree must "be drenched with the dew of heaven" (Daniel 4:15): it is a natural blessing that waters it.
2. By extension, dew refers to the water or humidity that falls and flows from the sky, wetting and soaking. When Nebuchadnezzar is turned into a beast and lives in the fields, "his body was drenched with the dew of heaven" (Daniel 4:33, 5:21): he is exposed to all the elements, soaked by the night humidity, like the beasts of the fields.
3. Figuratively, dew evokes lowering, humiliation, and exposure to the most lowly condition. It signifies here Nebuchadnezzar's state: a king reduced to living like the beasts, his body trembling under the dew, losing his royal dignity.
H2920.origine: The Aramaic word "tal" (טַל) comes directly from ancient Semitic and refers to the beneficial humidity that descends each night. The same word exists in Hebrew (טַל, tal) and carries the same concrete meaning: dew. It is a simple and natural word, drawn from the daily observation of the Mediterranean and Middle Eastern climate, where morning dew is a precious source of water. Dew often symbolizes in the Bible what comes from heaven, divine blessing, or, conversely, lowering when one is covered by it.
H2920.emploi: The word "dew" appears 5 times in the Bible, all occurrences in Aramaic in the book of Daniel, chapters 4 and 5, during the account of Nebuchadnezzar's madness. It appears in the prophetic dream (Daniel 4:15 and 4:23), where it refreshes the fallen tree but whose trunk survives, then in the fulfillment of the prophecy (Daniel 4:25, 4:33, 5:21). In each occurrence, Nebuchadnezzar, transformed into a creature living like the beasts, has "his body drenched with the dew of heaven": the dew emphasizes here his total stripping, his exposure to the natural elements, and his humiliating lowering. It is both a realistic detail and a symbol of divine humiliation.
H2920.portee: This image of dew falling on Nebuchadnezzar reminds us that even the most powerful of kings is subject to the elements and the will of God. The humiliation of the Assyrian king, drenched in dew like a beast of the fields, shows that human power is fragile and that God alone is sovereign. For the Christian reader, this invites humility and recognition that all honor, comfort, and status come from God and can be taken away to bring us back to wisdom.

sens: To present spots or marks of different colors
To have stripes or alternating patterns
To be sprinkled with parts of varied shades
To patch, repair by adding pieces
H2921.detail:
1. The main meaning is to have or bear distinct spots: "spotted" animals are marked with several colors, as in the account where Jacob chooses for wages the "spotted and speckled" lambs (Genesis 30:32), meaning those with white or colored marks on their fleece.
2. The word also refers to stripes or more complex patterns: the sheep that "bore young that were streaked, speckled, and spotted" (Genesis 30:39) show animals adorned with several types of interwoven marks.
3. The idea extends to fabrics: the "fabrics of all colors" (Ezekiel 16:16) are spotted fabrics, with diverse and variegated shades.
4. By extension, the verb can mean "to patch up," as in shoes that have been "repaired" (Joshua 9:5) where worn pieces have been added: here the spotting comes from the accumulation of patches and repairs.
H2921.origine: The Hebrew root טָלָא evokes the idea of marking, spotting, creating a visible pattern by adding elements. The word belongs to a family of terms describing variations in color and visible marks on a surface. The basic image is that of spots or added pieces that create a contrast with the surrounding surface.
H2921.emploi: The verb appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the account of Jacob's flocks in Genesis 30. In this pastoral context, it describes the animals with spotted and striped coats that Jacob claims as wages (Genesis 30:32-35, 39). It is always about visually distinguishing the beasts by their colored marks. In Joshua 9:5, it changes meaning and refers to faction shoes that have been patched multiple times. In Ezekiel 16:16, the metaphorical context of judgment against Jerusalem applies the word to the "colored fabrics" with which the city adorned itself. Each time, the emphasis is on visibility, distinction, or the combination of varied elements.
H2921.portee: This word reminds us that ordinary life — the flock animals, worn clothing, the adornment of cities — is noticed and important in God's eyes. In Jacob's story, the spotted animals symbolize divine blessing, while the patching speaks of human fragility and the wear of time. For the Christian, spotting evokes how God discerns the details of creation and our lives, and how our imperfections and repairs are part of the story that God writes.

sens: Young male or female sheep, domestic animal
The lamb as a sacrificial offering
Vulnerable or innocent person in need of protection
H2922.detail:
1. The lamb is a young sheep, a small, gentle, and innocent animal. In Isaiah 40:11, we see them "carried in the bosom" of the shepherd, an image of care and tenderness: it is a fragile animal that must be kept close.

2. The Bible often uses the lamb as a victim for sacrifices at the temple — an image of innocence offered to God. The word frequently appears in sacrifice accounts and in laws regarding worship.

3. Figuratively, the lamb represents one who is defenseless, guiltless, submissive — which is why the lamb becomes the symbol of one who suffers unjustly, an image taken up by Christ in the New Testament.
H2922.origine: The Hebrew word טְלָא (telah) is a variant of טָלֶה (taleh), both simply designating the young sheep. The root is ancient and common to Semitic languages. These slightly different forms are found in the Old Testament without distinction of meaning: it is a doublet, two ways of writing the same word.
H2922.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 40:11, in a poem of consolation where the Lord is compared to a shepherd. The verse speaks of the lambs — the smallest, most fragile of the flock — that the shepherd lifts and carries tenderly against his heart. It is an image of divine care for the weak. The use of the plural "lambs" emphasizes that God cares for all the little ones, the vulnerable of His people.
H2922.portee: This verse paints the Lord as a shepherd attentive to each, especially the weak and the needy. For the Christian reader, it reminds us that God never despises the small, the fragile, or those who can do nothing for themselves. It is a word of comfort: if you feel helpless or vulnerable, the Lord carries you in His tenderness, just as a shepherd carries newborn lambs.

sens: Place in Judah where King Saul gathered his troops
H2923.detail: Thelaim is a place located in Judah, in the southern kingdom of Israel. It is where King Saul summoned and reviewed his army before launching his attack against the Amalekites. The name means "lambs" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking a pastoral landscape or a place known for its flocks. Saul gathered 200,000 foot soldiers and 10,000 warriors from Judah there, an imposing force intended to combat Israel's enemies.
H2923.origine: The name Thelaim comes from the Hebrew "telai" which means "lamb." It is a place name formed on this image, probably because the region was a pasture or hosted sheep flocks. This type of geographical name was common in ancient Israel.
H2923.emploi: Thelaim appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 15:4. It is the starting point of King Saul's campaign against the Amalekites, shortly after his anointing by the prophet Samuel. Scripture mentions this place to show the extent of the king's military mobilization and the strategic importance of the moment: Saul gathered a considerable army at Thelaim before engaging in battle.

sens: Young sheep, offspring of the ewe
Animal offered as a sacrifice to God
Image of gentleness and innocence
Symbol of peace and messianic harmony
H2924.detail:
1. The lamb is the young of the sheep: a domesticated animal raised for its wool and meat. It is a gentle and defenseless animal, easy to handle. In 1 Samuel 7:9, Samuel takes a nursing lamb (very young) to offer as a burnt offering to the Lord.
2. The lamb is the quintessential sacrificial animal in Israel's worship. It was offered to God to atone for sins, to give thanks, or to implore His help. Samuel uses it as a solemn offering accompanied by his prayer for Israel.
3. Through its innocence and natural gentleness, the lamb represents vulnerability and purity. This is why the Bible chooses it as an image of one who suffers without retaliation or who is a victim without guilt.
4. In the vision of messianic peace in Isaiah 65:25, the lamb grazes alongside the wolf, its natural predators — an image of the reconciliation and harmony that God will establish at the end of times on His holy mountain.
H2924.origine: The Hebrew word טָלֶה (taleh) designates the young of the ewe. It belongs to the family of names for domesticated animals and remains specific to the lamb (distinct from the adult ewe). This word reflects the importance of sheep farming in the pastoral and cultic life of Israel: the lamb was both a source of wealth, food, and the central offering of the sacrificial system.
H2924.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible translated into French. It always refers to a young sheep. In 1 Samuel 7:9, the lamb is offered as a burnt offering: it is a solemn act of worship where Samuel seeks divine help in the war against the Philistines. In Isaiah 65:25, the lamb figures in the prophetic vision of the new world, where all hostility will disappear and where predator and prey will live in peace. The lamb embodies here restored innocence and the gentleness of God's reign.
H2924.portee: The lamb reminds the believer that sin requires atonement, but also that God accepts our offerings when they come from a sincere heart. In the prophetic vision, the lamb invites us to hope for true peace, when God will transform the very hearts of the powerful and eliminate violence from the world.

sens: Action of throwing, launching
Violent projection of a person
Forced expulsion
H2925.detail:
1. The word denotes the action of throwing or launching something with force — the movement of a projectile being thrown. In Isaiah 22:17, the Lord says, "He will throw you with a vigorous throw": the image is one of force projecting violently.
2. It can also evoke the way in which a person is propelled away from oneself, as one throws an object: a forced and brutal projection. This explains why the word could also mean "captivity" — being thrown out of one's country, torn from one's land.
3. By extension, the word evokes expulsion or being set aside: being thrown, rejected, forcibly removed.
H2925.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the violent movement of projection. The primary image is very concrete: that of a hand throwing, of a force casting something or someone far from it. This same root is used for ordinary physical gestures (throwing stones, casting a net) as well as for images of rejection or violence.
H2925.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 22:17. It describes the threat that the Lord addresses to Shebna, the steward of the king: he will be thrown, rejected far from power with irresistible violence, "wrapped up like a ball" — an image of something worthless that is rolled and thrown away. The context suggests a humiliating and complete disgrace: the fall of a proud man.
H2925.portee: This passage shows that God's judgment on pride and abuse of power is real and active: whoever turns away from God will be forcefully rejected, like a worthless object. It is a warning about the seriousness of sin and a confidence that God does not indefinitely tolerate rebellion.

sens: To put a roof or covering on a structure
To shelter, protect by a roofing
H2926.detail:
1. The word describes the action of placing a covering, generally a roof, on a structure to close and protect it. In Nehemiah 3:15, Shallum "covered" the gate of the spring: he gave it a roof or covering to protect it from the elements and make it a sheltered passage.
2. In a figurative or broader sense, the verb can mean "to shelter" or "to protect" by placing something above. The image is that of the roof providing shelter.
H2926.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of covering and protecting. Its Aramaic equivalent, תְלַל (telal), means "to have shade" or "to be in the shade," which reinforces the image of protection by covering. The family of this word shares the theme of protective covering.
H2926.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Nehemiah 3:15. It relates to the work of reconstruction after the exile: Shallum repairs and covers the gate of the spring, meaning he builds its roof or closing structure. The context shows the very practical and concrete sense: it concerns building work in the restoration of the gates and walls of Jerusalem.
H2926.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of protection and shelter in both material and spiritual life. The reconstruction of the temple and the gates of Jerusalem, of which this verse is a part, symbolizes the restoration of the people and their protection under God's hand. The detail of this work shows that God cares about every stone, every gate, every roof — a lesson on the care that the Lord provides to those who return to Him.

sens: Place where one is sheltered from the sun
Protection, refuge offered by something that covers
H2927.detail:
1. The shadow is primarily the cool and dark place created by something that interposes between us and the sun — here, the thick foliage of a large tree. In Daniel 4:12, the beasts of the field "sheltered under its shadow": they found there the coolness and protection from the burning sun.
2. By extension, the shadow designates anything that provides refuge, protection: the foliage of the large tree becomes a living shelter for all animals and birds. The image evokes security and dependence — to live "in the shadow" of something means to depend on it, to trust in it.
H2927.origine: The Aramaic word תְלַל (telal) comes from a primitive Semitic root meaning to cover, to cast a shadow. It is a form we call "Aphel" — a way of intensifying the meaning of the verb — which here means: to allow something to have shade, or to give shade. In Hebrew, the cognate verb טָלַל (talal) carries the same meaning of protective covering.
H2927.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Aramaic, in the dream of Nebuchadnezzar reported in Daniel 4. In this context, the gigantic tree with extended branches offers its shadow to the animals of the earth: it is an image of power, generosity, and protection. The shadow is not merely a physical phenomenon here, but a gift — a shelter upon which all living things depend.
H2927.portee: The shadow of the great tree in Daniel illustrates a profound biblical principle: those who have power and strength have a duty to protect the weak. This word invites the reader to reflect on the responsibility towards those around us, and to recognize that we never live alone — we all live, in one way or another, in the shadow of something or someone else.

sens: City in southern Judah
H2928G.detail: Thelem is a city located in the extreme south of the region of Judah, in the Negev desert. It appears only once in the Bible, listed among the cities that the territory of Judah possessed at the time of Joshua (Joshua 15:24).
H2928G.origine: The name Thelem means "oppression" in Hebrew. It is a place name that perhaps reflects a geographical or historical characteristic of the site at the time of its formation, although the precise details escape us.
H2928G.emploi: Thelem appears only once in Scripture: in Joshua 15:24, in the list of cities in the territory allocated to the tribe of Judah. It is among the cities of the Negev, the desert region in the south. This enumeration is part of the process of dividing the territory among the tribes of Israel after the conquest of Canaan under Joshua's leadership.

sens: Porter among the exiles who returned to Jerusalem
Man from the time of the restoration of Israel after the Babylonian exile
H2928H.detail:
1. Thelem is a porter (gatekeeper) of the temple who is listed among the Israelites who returned from the Babylonian exile during the time of Ezra. His name is mentioned in the list of those who broke away from the mixed marriages forbidden by the Law (Ezra 10:24).
2. He represents a generation of Israelites who experienced exile and participated in the national and religious restoration of Judah upon their return from captivity.
H2928H.origine: The name Thelem means "oppression" in Hebrew, likely referring to the sufferings of the exile that the people had just endured. It is a name given to a man from this pivotal period when Israel was regaining its land and its worship.
H2928H.emploi: Thelem appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:24. He is cited as one of the porters of the temple among those who agreed to separate from their foreign wives during the religious reform led by Ezra after the return from exile. He is included in an important administrative list that shows the efforts to restore the religious purity of Israel.

sens: Chief of a family of temple porters
Descendant of a lineage of gatekeepers of the sanctuary
H2929.detail: 1. Thalmon is the name of the chief of a family of porters of the temple in Jerusalem during the time of the Exile and the Return. He first appears in 1 Chronicles 9:17, where he is listed among the porters with his brothers Shallum and Akkub, Shallum being the leader of this group. 2. His descendants are mentioned as having been part of those who returned from exile with Zerubbabel and continued to serve as porters of the temple during the days of Nehemiah and Ezra, holding their hereditary position as gatekeepers of the sanctuary (Nehemiah 11:19, 12:25).
H2929.origine: The name Thalmon literally means "oppressor." It comes from a Hebrew root that evokes repression or domination. This name fits within the context of the names of the Levitical families of temple servants who resumed their functions after the exile.
H2929.emploi: Thalmon appears five times in the biblical texts, always in relation to his role as a porter of the temple. He is first mentioned individually in 1 Chronicles 9:17 as one of the main porters of the pre-exilic period. His descendants are then listed in the return lists from exile (Ezra 2:42 and Nehemiah 7:45), where 138 or 139 sons of Thalmon are counted among the returning porters. Finally, in Nehemiah 11:19 and 12:25, he is found again among the temple gatekeepers during the time of reconstruction, confirming that his family continued its service role.

sens: To become or be unclean according to the rules of ritual purity of Israelite worship
To be contaminated by contact with something unclean (a corpse, a disease, an unclean animal)
To profane or violate a sacred commitment, particularly marriage or the name of God
To become unclean through the practice of idolatrous or immoral acts
H2930A.detail:
1. The primary meaning is cultic: a person or thing becomes "unclean" when it violates the purity rules established by the Law. This does not mean "dirty" in the physical sense, but "unfit to participate in worship." A woman who has her period is temporarily unclean (Leviticus 15:19); a leper is unclean as long as the lesion is not healed (Leviticus 13:14).
2. Impurity is transmitted by contact: whoever touches a reptile becomes unclean, as do their clothes and their bed (Leviticus 22:5). It is a ritual impurity, limited in time, which is purified by washing or waiting.
3. To defile can also mean "to dishonor" or "to violate": when Shechem defiles Dinah, he gravely offends her family and honor (Genesis 34:5). Illicit marriage or infidelity defiles.
4. The word also applies to moral and spiritual pollution: fathers have defiled their sons by enticing them to serve idols (Ezekiel 20:18). Here, to defile means "to pervert" and "to lead into sin."
H2930A.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of defect or stain. It also gives the adjective "unclean" (tamé), which describes what cannot enter the sanctuary or cannot be eaten according to the Law. The underlying notion is one of separation: the unclean is separated from the pure, the holy, the consecrated to God. In biblical thought, impurity is an objective ritual state that requires purification, distinct from moral guilt.
H2930A.emploi: The verb appears 142 times in the Old Testament, mainly in Leviticus (laws of ritual purity) and in Numbers. It describes the ceremonial impurity of the sick, women during menstruation, and those who touch a corpse or an unclean animal. Leviticus 11 and 15 provide concrete cases: those who eat or touch an unclean animal become unclean. The verb is also used to describe the violation of marriage (Genesis 34:5), the profanation of God's name through idolatry (Ezekiel 20:18), or the moral corruption brought by sin. Depending on the context, to defile refers to a temporary and ritual impurity, or a deep moral and spiritual stain.
H2930A.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, ritual purity is not a regulatory detail: it expresses the separation between the holy and the profane, and the respect due to God in worship. For the Christian, the purity laws of Leviticus find their meaning in Christ, who abolishes the cultic distinction but calls for the purity of heart. To defile also evokes the idea that sin distances us from God and renders us unfit for His presence, until we are purified by His forgiveness.

sens: that is not pure, that is defiled or contaminated
that violates a religious rule or a prohibition of the Law
that is morally or spiritually corrupt
that renders one who touches it unfit for worship
H2931.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a concrete defilement: a dead or sick animal that renders unclean the person or object that touches it (Leviticus 5:2). The defilement is transmitted by contact, like a contamination (Numbers 19:22).
2. It applies to animals that the Law declares unclean because they do not meet the purity criteria: certain rodents, reptiles, or animals without split hooves (Leviticus 11:29). These animals are regarded as unclean, meaning they are classified as such according to the category established by God.
3. The word describes ritually unclean diseases or sores: leprosy that defiles (Leviticus 13:44 to 13:46), a house whose affliction spreads and becomes unclean (Leviticus 14:44 to 14:45).
4. In a moral and spiritual sense, it expresses the internal corruption of the being: the psalmist acknowledges, "Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?" (Job 14:4), and the prophet Isaiah exclaims, "Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips" (Isaiah 6:5). Impurity then is the moral defect that distances us from God.
H2931.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that carries the idea of staining, marking, or defiling. It is related to the image of something that is tarnished or darkened. Ritual impurity in the Old Testament is not sin in the moral sense, but a condition of separation from the sacred: one who is unclean must purify themselves through time, washing, or sacrifice before approaching the sanctuary. It is a system of classifications that protects the holiness of the temple and the people of God.
H2931.emploi: The word appears 78 times, concentrated in Leviticus (the great law of purity) and scattered throughout Exodus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy. It describes four main categories: unclean animals that cannot be eaten (Leviticus 11:4 to 11:8), skin diseases and discharges that render unclean (Leviticus 13 to 15), corpses and the dead (Numbers 19:13 to 19:22), and secondarily the moral and spiritual (Job 14:4; Isaiah 6:5). From book to book, the word retains its meaning of separation from the pure, but it enriches: it moves from practical ritual to the awareness of moral sin.
H2931.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that purity is important in the relationship with God. Although the ritual laws no longer apply to Christians, they signal a lasting truth: we are all spiritually defiled by sin, and we need purification. Jesus Christ, through His sacrifice and His blood, purifies us from all moral and spiritual impurity. This word helps to understand the urgency of grace and the importance of sanctification in the Christian life.

sens: State of what is physically contaminated or stained
Discharge or flow from the body
Moral or religious transgression
Disobedience that separates from God and His worship
H2932.detail:
1. Impurity primarily refers to a concrete stain or physical contamination: when one touches a corpse or a repugnant substance, one becomes impure (Leviticus 5:3). It is a reality of the body.
2. It includes bodily discharges, particularly menstrual flows or others: a woman who has a flow is impure for the entire duration of the flow, just as during her period (Leviticus 15:25).
3. Impurity extends to moral and religious fault: it designates the state of one who disobeys God's law. This is why God calls for purification from impurity, as the people did after the exile (Ezekiel 36:25).
4. It also signifies the state of separation from God: one who is impure cannot enter the temple or participate in worship, for impurity distances one from divine holiness. The impurity of the pagan nations even contaminates the land they occupy (Ezra 9:11).
H2932.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of being hidden, obscured, or darkened. Impurity is what veils, what tarnishes. It is linked to the biblical concept of holiness: what is holy must be separated from what defiles. It is an exclusively Hebrew word, central to the ritualized system of the Law.
H2932.emploi: The word impurity appears 31 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the books of the Law (Leviticus and Numbers) that establish the rules of ritual purity. It designates very varied realities: contact with death, bodily discharges (menstruation, discharge of a sick woman), consumption of forbidden foods, and more broadly, sin and moral transgression. In Ezekiel, impurity especially becomes an image of the people's sin: the prophet speaks of the impurity of the heart and the idolatrous behavior of Israel. In the context of vows (Judges 13:7), eating something impure breaks the consecration to God. Thus, impurity is progressive: from the ritual to the moral, from physical stain to spiritual guilt.
H2932.portee: Understanding impurity helps the Christian see that the Bible takes sin seriously: evil is not just an invisible fault, it is a reality that defiles and distances one from God. For the Israelite, the rules of purity constantly reminded them that one must be separated from evil to approach God. For today's believer, this sheds light on the need for moral and spiritual purification that only Christ can accomplish (Titus 2:14).

sens: To have one's course interrupted, to stop abruptly
To be blocked, obstructed
To be treated as impure, despised
H2933.detail:
1. The word first evokes something that stops, that can no longer advance: a current of water that no longer flows, a breath that interrupts. In Job 18:3, the context of "beasts" suggests this idea: why does our understanding stop? Why do you no longer listen to us?
2. The primary meaning can also designate a blocked conduit, an opening that is obstructed and prevents passage. It is the physical image of an interruption.
3. By extension, the word acquires a figurative sense: to be treated as something blocked, closed, unworthy of attention. To be considered as impure or despicable is to be stopped in one's dignity, excluded from respect. The context of Job with "beasts," "brutes" reinforces this nuance: to be reduced to nothing in the eyes of others.
H2933.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root expressing the idea of interruption and blockage.
