The niphal form (the passive voice in Hebrew) indicates that the subject undergoes the action: he is stopped, interrupted, rather than he stops someone. This root can also evoke the notion of dirtiness or ritual impurity in certain biblical contexts, hence the link with "impure": what is blocked, hindered, is also what cannot circulate, pass the filter.
H2933.emploi: The word appears only once in Job 18:3. Job defends himself against his friends who seem to treat him with disdain. Their gaze upon him stops him, blocks him, reduces him to silence or contempt. The use of the verb here is not technical or ritual (as in the laws of purity), but deeply human: it is the experience of one who feels judged, despised, deprived of dignity by the gaze of others.
H2933.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader how a human being can feel "stopped" or "closed" by the judgment of others — or by their own guilt. It invites reflection on how we look at those who suffer and to recognize that every person, even the miserable, remains worthy of listening to and respect. It is a lesson in compassion in the face of contempt.

sens: To put or place something out of sight, in a secret or underground place
To plunge, insert, or embed in a substance
To set or stretch a trap, a net by concealing
To hide oneself, to evade sight
To keep hidden, to reserve secretly
H2934.detail:
1. To put something out of sight: this is placing an object in a location where it will not be found. Jacob buried the foreign gods under an oak tree (Genesis 35:4), and Achan hides the stolen goods in the ground in the midst of his tent (Joshua 7:21).
2. To plunge or embed in a substance: this means to insert deeply, like the sluggard who plunges his hand into the dish of food (Proverbs 26:15).
3. To set a trap by concealing: this is placing a net, a cord, or traps in a hidden manner to catch someone by surprise. The wicked lay traps in secret (Psalms 64:6) and the nations fall into the net they have hidden (Psalms 9:16).
4. To hide oneself, to evade: this is to place oneself out of sight voluntarily to avoid being discovered.
5. To keep hidden, to reserve: this is to keep something secret or in reserve, held away from view.
H2934.origine: The verb comes from a Semitic root expressing the idea of covering, occluding, or embedding. This root is related to the concrete image of placing something underground or out of shelter. The word evokes darkness and concealment, whether accidental or intentional.
H2934.emploi: This verb appears 29 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical narratives (Genesis, Joshua), Psalms, and Proverbs. In the narratives, it describes the action of securing (one buries idols) or stealing clandestinely (Achan hides the spoils). The Psalms use it for the traps of enemies or hidden malice: the wicked lay their traps in secret. Proverbs uses it for images of laziness or concealment. The word can also describe physical embedding in a substance.
H2934.portee: This word reminds us that secret acts are never truly hidden before God. The traps that enemies lay in secret come back to them (Psalms 9:16), and even what is buried underground can be discovered, like Achan's sin. For the believer, this invites transparency and awareness that nothing escapes him, just as the truth cannot remain buried forever.

sens: Woven or knitted container for carrying or storing fruits and crops
Symbol of divine blessing or curse on the harvest and prosperity
H2935.detail:
1. A basket is a container, typically made of wicker or woven material, used for gathering, transporting, and presenting the fruits of the earth. In the Law of Moses, the people were to fill a basket with the first fruits and bring it to the sanctuary as an offering to God (Deuteronomy 26:2-4).
2. The basket also becomes an image of all the wealth it symbolizes: when God "blesses" it, it signifies that the entire harvest and food prosper; when He "curses" it, famine threatens (Deuteronomy 28:5, 17). This is why the basket concretely represents the abundance or scarcity that the Lord sends.
H2935.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of weaving or braiding. Its primary image is that of a manufactured object, a construction of interwoven fibers. The basket is typically a utensil of agricultural daily life, very common among the farmers and shepherds of ancient Israel.
H2935.emploi: This word appears 4 times in the Segond, exclusively in Deuteronomy, at the heart of two legal passages. First, in Deuteronomy 26, it designates the specific container where the Israelite must place his first fruits to offer them at the sanctuary — it is a prescription of worship and acknowledgment towards God. Then, in Deuteronomy 28, the "basket" becomes the symbol of the material blessing of the faithful people, or conversely, of their curse if they stray from the Lord. The concrete object thus takes on a theological significance: it crystallizes God's promise to provide or withhold.
H2935.portee: The basket reminds the believer that all prosperity comes from God and must first be offered to Him. The obligation to bring the first fruits in a basket to the sanctuary teaches that our possessions do not wholly belong to us: they are received, and God expects our gratitude and obedience. Blessing and curse on the basket also show that the believer's relationship with God determines his material security.

sens: to make dirty, to cover with dirt or filth
to morally stain, to tarnish someone's honor or purity
H2936.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of making something dirty or impure by covering it with dust, mud, or other substances. In the Song of Songs, the young woman refuses to soil her feet that she has just washed (Song of Songs 5:3): the image is concrete and sensual, that of bare feet that would be soiled by contact with the ground or the street.
2. In a figurative sense, the word expresses a moral or spiritual impurity, an affront to purity or dignity. Although this second sense is implicit in biblical Hebrew, it is rooted in the same logic: what is pure must not be exposed to what is impure or degrading.
H2936.origine: The Hebrew verb נִפַל (ta.naph) belongs to the family of words that evoke dirtiness and loss of purity. It is used in the Piel form (an intensive form) to emphasize the action of soiling. In the Greek Old Testament, this type of impurity is often rendered by verbs meaning "to contaminate" or "to make impure," in connection with the purity laws of Leviticus.
H2936.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the Song of Songs 5:3. It is a moment of poetic intimacy where the young woman hesitates to grant favors to the one she loves, fearing to spoil the purity of her gestures and her body. The context is one of tender modesty and delicate reluctance, where "to soil" rhymes with "to give oneself" or "to submit again." This rare term underscores the importance placed in the poem on the cleanliness and integrity of the beloved body.
H2936.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on purity — both physical and spiritual — and on the care taken to preserve what is precious. In the dynamic of the Song, it also illustrates how true love requires restraint and mutual respect: to soil the purity of another is to wound them. For the Christian, this passage can shed light on the importance of preserving one's integrity and that of others in relationships.

sens: to wander, to stray from the path
to deceive someone, to lead them away from the truth
to seduce, to lead someone into error
H2937.detail:
1. The verb first evokes the act of losing oneself, of leaving the right path, physically or morally. It describes one who wanders without a guide, who goes astray.
2. When it comes to leading someone astray (the sense used in the Bible), the word means to deceive, to mislead. The prophet Ezekiel denounces the false prophets who "lead astray" the people of God by proclaiming "Peace!" when there is no peace (Ezekiel 13:10): they divert him from the truth and lead him toward false confidence.
3. Thus, it also carries the idea of moral seduction: leading someone into error, lies, idolatry, or disobedience to God.
H2937.origine: The Hebrew root טעה (ta'ah) paints the image of one who strays, who deviates from their path. The Hiphil (a form that makes the notion of deviation active) transforms this meaning: instead of straying oneself, one causes another to stray. It is the act of one who deliberately leads astray.
H2937.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible in the active sense, in Ezekiel 13:10. There, God condemns the prophets of Jerusalem who "lead astray" His people. They do so by telling him soothing words ("Peace!") while judgment approaches, thus diverting him from repentance. This context shows that leading astray is not innocent: it is a conscious deception that has serious spiritual consequences. The false prophets become responsible for the people's blindness.
H2937.portee: This word challenges the role of those who teach or lead: they can lead the people of God into error either through ignorance or deliberate lies. For the reader, it serves as a warning against those who proclaim a false peace, an illusory security. It also invites discernment regarding who truly speaks the word of God and who distorts it. Faithfulness to God's truth is a protection against being led astray.

sens: To put in the mouth and perceive the flavor of a food or drink
To eat or drink a small amount
To perceive, discern, experience something
To appreciate, to take pleasure in something
H2938.detail:
1. To taste is primarily to put something in the mouth to feel its flavor. Jonathan tastes a bit of honey, and his eyes brighten immediately: the honey has such a pleasant flavor that it physically revives him (1 Samuel 14:29). It is a simple and direct action: perceiving through the palate.
2. To taste can also mean to eat or drink, at least a small amount. David refuses to taste bread before sunset as a sign of mourning: to taste here means to eat (2 Samuel 3:35). It is a concrete act of nourishing one's body.
3. The image of the palate discerning the flavors of food becomes an image of perception and understanding. Just as the ear discerns words, the palate savors food, says Job: both function in the same way, perceiving and judging (Job 12:11). It is the transition from the physical to the mental.
4. Finally, to taste takes on a broader meaning: to experience, to appreciate something. An eighty-year-old servant asks if he can still savor what he eats and drinks: to savor is not only to eat but also to enjoy, to take pleasure (2 Samuel 19:35). The idea of enjoyment and satisfaction is at the heart of the word.
H2938.origine: The Hebrew verb ta'am comes from a root that describes the act of tasting with the mouth and palate. It is a concrete word that arises from the daily experience of eating. The derived noun ta'am means flavor, taste, or judgment, showing how Hebrew easily transitions from physical sensation to the ability to discern and judge. The Aramaic parallel, te'am ('to feed'), reveals the close relationship between tasting and nourishing: to taste is already to eat, at least a little.
H2938.emploi: This verb appears ten times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical books (1 and 2 Samuel, 3 occurrences) and in wisdom literature (Job, Psalms, Proverbs, 5 occurrences). The concrete uses dominate initially: Jonathan tastes honey, David refuses to taste bread (1 Samuel 14:29, 43; 2 Samuel 3:35). Then the image extends to less material realities: can a servant still savor food at eighty years old (2 Samuel 19:35)? The palate savors food just as the ear discerns words (Job 12:11; 34:3). In the later uses provided (Psalms 34:9; Proverbs 31:18; Jonah 3:7), the word touches on spiritual and moral domains: to taste can mean to experience the goodness of the Lord. Thus, the word gradually rises from the physical to the spiritual.
H2938.portee: To taste invites the Christian to move from mere consumption to true perception, true appreciation. When the Bible speaks of tasting the goodness of the Lord, it calls for more than a vague belief: it calls for a personal, concrete, flavorful experience. It is a word that connects body and soul, the sensitive palate and the discerning mind. It reminds us that our relationship with God engages all our senses and our entire consciousness.

sens: To consume food
To feed, nourish
H2939.detail:
1. To consume food: this is the action of taking food and ingesting it. In Daniel 4:25, King Nebuchadnezzar, having become like a beast, will receive "grass to eat" like the oxen, an image of his total humiliation and reduction to an animal state.
2. To feed, nourish: the word can also refer to the action of providing food to someone or to an animal. The same scene in Daniel 5:21 specifies that "he was given grass to eat like the oxen," emphasizing that his very survival depended on the divine will that nourished him despite his downfall.
H2939.origine: This Aramaic word derives from the Hebrew verb טָעַם (taam), which means "to taste" or "to try." The meaning has broadened: to taste is primarily to put in the mouth, hence the idea of eating and taking food. Aramaic uses the same root with the more general sense of "to eat" or "to be nourished." This family of words reminds us that tasting and eating are linked: one must taste what one eats.
H2939.emploi: The word appears three times in the book of Daniel, all in the account of Nebuchadnezzar's punishment. In Daniel 4:25 and 4:32, we find the parallel expression "you will be given grass to eat like the oxen," describing how the king, driven among the beasts of the field, will be reduced to eating grass like an animal. Daniel 5:21 recounts the same idea in the past tense. In these three contexts, the verb illustrates the extreme humiliation of the monarch: deprived of his humanity, power, and royal dignity, he can only eat like the beasts.
H2939.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that even the greatest kings of this world are subject to the will of the Most High. The spectacle of Nebuchadnezzar reduced to eating the grass of the fields shows that human pride is fragile: he who refuses to acknowledge the supreme God can be lowered below the animal. It is a call to humility and the fear of God, who "rules over the kingdom of men and gives it to whom He wills."

sens: Perceptible flavor in the mouth when eating or drinking
Ability to discern, to judge, to appreciate
Good sense, wise judgment in a given situation
Decision, order, judgment from an authority
H2940.detail:
1. Taste is primarily the flavor we perceive when we eat: the manna had the taste of a honey cake (Exodus 16:31), and elsewhere that of a cake baked in oil (Numbers 11:8). It is the physical sensation of the palate.
2. Taste also becomes the ability to discern, to have judgment in serious matters. David thanks Abigail: her sagacity prevented him from committing a vengeful murder (1 Samuel 25:33). It is the intelligence that knows how to appreciate what is fitting.
3. Good sense or practical sagacity of a person: the aged can be deprived of it by God (Job 12:20), losing this faculty of judgment. It is discernment, reason.
4. Finally, taste denotes an order, a decision emanating from an authority: Jonah receives the order from the king of Nineveh (Jonah 3:7). It is a judgment that imposes itself, a decree.
H2940.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to feel," "to perceive." Taste was understood as a form of perception and discernment: one tastes with the mouth, but one also "tastes" a counsel or a situation with intelligence. The same image applies to judgment: the one who judges "tastes" the facts first before deciding. In the Greek Bible, this word corresponds to the Greek γεύομαι (to taste) and the words for judgment and discernment.
H2940.emploi: This word appears twelve times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Wisdom literature (Job, Proverbs, Psalms) and a few narratives. The concrete sense of flavor dominates in the accounts of the manna (Exodus, Numbers). The sense of judgment or discernment appears in Proverbs and Job, where it denotes sagacity, good sense: a beautiful woman but devoid of discernment is compared to a sow (Proverbs 11:22). The order or royal decree is closely related: the king of Nineveh publishes a judgment (Jonah 3:7). To counterfeit the foolish (1 Samuel 21:13) means to act without judgment, as if one had lost discernment.
H2940.portee: The word reminds us that wisdom is also a form of perception and sensation: we discern good from evil as we discern tastes. For the Christian, cultivating spiritual taste means learning to discern what is good and pleasing to God. It also recognizes that God's order imposes itself on our lives as a sovereign word.

sens: Decision, order, command issued by an authority
Report, account addressed to a superior
Discretion, ability to assess and judge
H2941.detail:
1. This word primarily refers to a decision or judgment rendered by someone in authority: an order, a directive (Ezra 5:5, where it speaks of sending a report to King Darius, who will judge it).
2. It also means an account, a report, an explanation given to a superior to justify what one has done (Daniel 6:2: the satraps must report to Daniel, who himself answers to the king).
3. By extension, it refers to the capacity for discernment, judgment, the ability to weigh matters and decide wisely.
H2941.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the root "ta.am" (טעם), which primarily means "to taste." Just as taste allows the tongue to distinguish flavors, judgment enables the mind to discern and decide: it is a very natural image in the Semitic world. The word has thus extended from "taste" to "discernment," then to "judgment" and "order."
H2941.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Aramaic Bible. In both cases, it is in the context of Persian power and authority reporting. In Ezra 5:5, it refers to sending a report to King Darius before rendering accounts to him. In Daniel 6:2, it refers to the duty that the satraps have to report to Daniel. It is always a term of imperial and judicial administration.
H2941.portee: This word reminds us that all judgment and authority involve responsibility: those who command must give accounts, even kings. It is a lesson in biblical wisdom: power is never absolute, and even the great must justify their actions.

sens: Command given by an authority
Official decision or permission granted
Royal decree or edict
Judgment, opinion or sensible advice
H2942.detail:
1. Order in the sense of command: an instruction given by someone in authority, as when King Darius orders searches in the archives (Ezra 6:1), or when King Nebuchadnezzar commands all peoples to bow down before the statue (Daniel 3:10).
2. Official authorization: the formal permission granted by an authority to carry out an action, as when the elders ask Zerubbabel who gave him permission to build the house of God (Ezra 5:9).
3. Royal decree: a solemn ordinance from a king that is binding on all his subjects, particularly in the books of Ezra and Daniel where the Persian and Babylonian kings issue edicts (Ezra 6:11, Daniel 6:26).
4. Wise or sensible judgment: a well-founded opinion, a way of acting with discernment and prudence, as when Daniel speaks sensibly to the chief of the guards (Daniel 2:14).
H2942.origine: The Hebrew word teem comes from a root that fundamentally means "to taste" or "to sense." This basic image explains its two meanings: one tastes something to judge its quality, hence the idea of judgment and opinion; and one also tastes in the sense of experiencing or recognizing something, hence the idea of order or official decision that is made known. The notion of prudent judgment remains present even in the usages in the sense of royal order.
H2942.emploi: This word appears 26 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the books of Ezra and Daniel, which recount the events of the captivity and restoration of Israel under the Babylonian and Persian empires. It consistently refers to either an order from a royal authority (King Darius, King Nebuchadnezzar) or an official authorization. In Ezra 6:11 and Daniel 3:10, teem takes the form of a royal edict that engages the responsibility of the sovereign and must be executed. In Daniel 2:14, the meaning nuances towards that of a sensible and wise word. The usage reflects the historical context well: Israel, subjected to foreign powers, must obey the orders of its masters.
H2942.portee: This word reminds believers that even in exile, even under the reign of pagan kings, God governs events. The orders of kings allow Israel to rebuild the temple and return to Jerusalem. For us today, teem invites us to discern between just and unjust orders: to obey legitimate authorities in what they command that is just, but also to know that only God's order is definitive.

sens: Place a burden on the back of a beast of burden
H2943.detail: 1. To load means to place a burden, provisions, or luggage on the back of an animal (donkey, camel, mule) for transport. In the account of Genesis 45:17, Pharaoh orders Joseph's brothers to load their animals with provisions before they leave for the land of Canaan: it is the practical and daily action of preparing the animals for a journey, putting on their backs everything that needs to be transported.
H2943.origine: The Hebrew verb טָעַן (ta'an) comes from a root that denotes the action of physically loading, placing a burden. It is a concrete word, derived from the vocabulary of the nomadic and pastoral life of the ancient Near East, where transport by beasts of burden was the primary method of moving goods and families.
H2943.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Genesis 45:17. It occurs at a key moment in the narrative: after Joseph reveals himself to his brothers, Pharaoh himself acknowledges his dignity and orders that they prepare for their journey back to Canaan. The word expresses the practical and urgent action of loading the animals for departure, in a context of family reconciliation and generous provision.
H2943.portee: This small word illustrates how the concrete details of travel and transport punctuate the grand biblical narratives. It reminds us that biblical faith does not disdain material realities and that God is also concerned with the practical organization of His people's lives, including their provisioning along the way.

sens: To pierce, to stab with a sharp or pointed weapon
H2944.detail: 1. This word evokes the action of piercing a body with a weapon — sword, spear, or arrow. In Isaiah 14:19, it describes the "blows" of the sword that have pierced the bodies of the slain warriors: the image is one of penetrating, violent, and deadly wounds.
H2944.origine: The root literally means "to pierce" or "to stab." It is used to describe the action of striking with a sharp or pointed weapon that penetrates the flesh.
H2944.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 14:19, within the prophetic oracle against the king of Babylon. It characterizes the state of the dead in battle — bodies pierced by swords, humiliated and thrown away like unhonored corpses, cast into a pit without a proper burial.
H2944.portee: This word reminds the reader of the brutal reality of death in battle and, in this prophetic context, the humiliated fall of the proud tyrant. It underscores that even the most powerful kings will meet an undignified end.

sens: Infant, small child
Children of a family, a people, group of the youngest
Children and women, meaning vulnerable and non-combatant individuals
H2945.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to very young children, the little ones, those who need protection and care. In Genesis 50:21, Joseph tells his brothers that he will provide for "you and your children," indicating those who depend on the head of the family.
2. It applies to all the children of a person or a people, the youngest members of the group. In Deuteronomy 1:39, the Lord speaks of the "little children" who will enter Canaan because they "do not yet know good from evil" — these are the future generations, innocent of their parents' rebellion.
3. In contexts of war or captivity, "children" regularly refers to vulnerable individuals — women, children, and the elderly — who are not fought against but are kept or massacred. In Numbers 31:9, "the women of the Midianites with their little children" are taken captive, and in Exodus 10:10, Pharaoh refuses to let the little ones accompany the men into the desert.
H2945.origine: The Hebrew word טַף (taph) is related to the idea of something small, weak, fragile — one who needs to be carried. The root evokes childhood as a state of natural dependence. It is distinct from בֵן (ben), "son," which emphasizes fatherhood and lineage, and from יֶלֶד (yèled), which refers more to the young child by essence. טַף emphasizes vulnerability and the need for protection.
H2945.emploi: The word appears 42 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books (from Genesis to Deuteronomy) and in exile narratives. It is very frequent in contexts of migration and settlement: when families move (Exodus 12:37: "about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides children"), when taking territory (Deuteronomy 2:34: "we took all its cities, and we devoted to destruction... the women and the children"), or when gathering the people (Deuteronomy 29:11: "your children"). The meaning is constant: the youngest and most vulnerable of the group. Its usage reveals the importance that the Bible places on passing on to future generations.
H2945.portee: This word reminds us that God cares for the weakest and smallest. The emphasis on children in the narratives of the Desert and conquest shows that God thinks of the future of the people, not just the present generation. It is a call to protect and educate children, for they are the future and the continuation of the divine promise.

sens: to unfold, to open wide
to care for someone by carrying or nourishing them
H2946.detail:
1. To extend means to unfold something by opening or spreading it wide. It is the gesture of someone who unfolds a fabric, or here, who extends the heavens as one extends a hand. In Isaiah 48:13, God says: "My right hand has extended the heavens" — He speaks of the creative act by which He has unfolded the vastness of the sky.
2. To extend can also mean to care for a person tenderly, particularly by carrying or nourishing them when they are small or weak. The word evokes the image of someone carrying a child in their arms or on their hands to pamper and help them grow. In Lamentations 2:22, the prophet laments: "Those whom I had cared for and raised, my enemy has consumed" — he speaks of the children he has carried and nourished with devotion.
H2946.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from the root טפח which primarily evokes the idea of lightly striking or taking small quick steps — like the small steps of a child. From there comes the meaning of extending hands to welcome or carry something or someone. The same root also expresses the idea of unfolding: extending arms, extending the heavens.
H2946.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Isaiah 48:13, it describes the divine creative act: God extends the heavens with His right hand, an image of His power that shapes the universe. In Lamentations 2:22, it means to care for and raise a child tenderly, by carrying them. These two usages — one majestic and cosmic, the other maternal and familiar — reveal the richness of the word: to unfold, to open wide, and through tenderness, to carry.
H2946.portee: This word reminds the believer that the same God who created and unfolded the entire universe with His hand also knows the intimate care of a parent for a child. It unites celestial grandeur and the gentleness of daily care: God who extends the heavens is also the One who carries and nourishes His children.

sens: The width of a hand, about four fingers
A unit of measure based on this width
The thickness of an object or a wall
The molding or cornice that crowns a wall or a structure
H2947.detail:
1. The palm is primarily the width of the human hand, from the thumb to the little finger spread apart — about four fingers wide, or 7 to 8 centimeters. It is a natural and easy measure to use on a construction site: everyone could verify it on their own body.
2. As a unit, it serves to measure lengths or thicknesses. In the large bronze basin of Solomon's temple, it specifies that "its thickness was a palm" (1 Kings 7:26): the metal forming the walls is the thickness of a hand.
3. The word can also simply refer to the thickness of something, like the dimension between two opposing surfaces.
4. In architecture, the palm refers to a cornice or molding — the band that runs along a wall or facade, often protruding. In Jerusalem, Solomon's temple was adorned with these cornices: "internally and externally" (1 Kings 7:9).
H2947.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root that means "to strike" or "to hit" — the basic idea is that of a width that can be covered or reached with a hand's span. It is an anthropomorphic measure, based on the human body as a natural standard, like many ancient measures (cubit, finger, foot).
H2947.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts of measurement or construction. Twice, it describes the thickness of the walls of the bronze basin of the temple (1 Kings 7:26 and 2 Chronicles 4:5) — the text establishes that they measure a palm in thickness. Once, it designates the cornices of the house in Jerusalem (1 Kings 7:9): these architectural moldings that complete a facade. Finally, in Psalm 39:6, the psalmist uses the word figuratively to express the brevity of human life: "You have given my days the width of a hand" — a poignant metaphor: our years last only the span of a palm, an insignificant measure before eternity.
H2947.portee: This word invites the believer to meditate on the brevity of earthly life. The psalmist uses the concrete image of a palm — a measure that can be covered by a finger — to remind us that human existence, no matter how active or ambitious, occupies only an infinitesimal width in divine time. It directs towards humility and the pursuit of what lasts: communion with God.

sens: A unit of measurement equal to the width of an open hand, from the little finger to the thumb
A narrow edge or border that surrounds an object
A narrow margin or transition between two spaces
H2948.detail:
1. The span is a measure of length based on the human body: it is the distance that separates the little finger from the thumb when the hand is fully spread. In Ezekiel 40:5, this measure is used to assess the cubits of the Temple: "each cubit having a span more than the ordinary cubit" — the span is added to the standard unit. It is a practical and universal measure, as everyone carries their hand with them.
2. The span also refers to the narrow edge that borders the sacred furniture. On the sacrificial tables of the Temple, "four fingers' breadth were fitted to the house all around" (Ezekiel 40:43): this span prevents the offerings from slipping. Similarly, the table of showbread had "a border of four fingers" (Exodus 25:25), bordered with gold to enhance its beauty.
3. Figuratively, the span represents an intermediate area or a contour that completes a structure: the altar of the Temple had "a border that finished its outline" (Ezekiel 43:13), marking the transition between its pedestal and its main surface.
H2948.origine: The Hebrew word טֹפַח comes from a root that evokes the action of opening or spreading the hand. The span is an anthropomorphic measure — it takes the human body as a reference, just like the cubit (the distance from the elbow to the fingers). It is a practical term used in the architectural descriptions of the Temple where the precision of proportions holds religious significance.
H2948.emploi: The word appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the descriptions of the Tabernacle and the Temple (Exodus and Ezekiel). In Exodus 25:25 and 37:12, it measures the borders of the sacred furniture. In Ezekiel's visions (40:5, 40:43, 43:13), it is used to assess the dimensions of the future Temple and to regulate the proportions of its altars. The word oscillates between two uses: linear measurement on one hand, and edge or border on the other — both meanings are related, as the border has precisely the thickness of a span.
H2948.portee: The span reminds us that God communicates with man through measures that man can verify with his own body. This humble and corporeal unit emphasizes that worship is not an abstraction: the Temple, its furniture, and its altars are built to human scale, accessible to the understanding and touch of the people. It is an invitation to see the hand of God in the order and proportion of holy things.

sens: Affectionate care given to a small child
Delicate and protective attention
Maternal affection towards what is fragile
H2949.detail:
1. The word denotes the tender care given to a small child: to pamper, to cuddle, to provide daily affection. In Lamentations 2:20, the poet speaks of the children who were "objects of tenderness," meaning nourished and loved devotedly by their mothers.
2. More broadly, it is the delicate attention given to something or someone fragile and vulnerable, a form of affectionate protection that manifests deep attachment.
H2949.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to mistreat, crush, strike," but in this context, it has taken on the meaning of "to treat with care" — as if "to care for" implies meticulous and delicate attention. The noun expresses the idea of maternal tenderness and devotion towards those we love.
H2949.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Lamentations 2:20. It is situated in a context of funeral lamentation over the destruction of Jerusalem: the poet recalls the children who were once the object of their mothers' tenderness, to highlight the horror of the siege, where these same children died of hunger or perished in the catastrophe. This word thus expresses both the sweetness of maternal love and, by contrast, the cruelty of their loss.
H2949.portee: This word helps us meditate on the vulnerability of children and on maternal love as a reflection of divine affection. In a context of catastrophe, it reminds us that the death of the innocent is an offense against the order created by God, and invites the believer to recognize the depth of human grief and suffering.

sens: To coat, cover with a layer
To apply, attach
To invent, forge from scratch
To accumulate accusations against someone
To meditate, form a plan
H2950.detail:
1. In its literal sense, the word evokes the action of coating a surface, covering it with a sticky or malleable substance: it is the gesture of the potter who coats, or the mason who plasters. This concrete sense of "to cover" provides the basic image of the word.

2. From there arises the sense of manufacturing, shaping: assembling elements to form a whole, as one glues pieces together. It is the idea of inventing or forging by composition.

3. In the three biblical passages provided, the word takes on the meaning of inventing or forging accusations: Job reproaches his friends for imagining "falsehoods" (Job 13:4), God "imagines iniquities" against Job (Job 14:17), and the proud "imagine falsehoods against me" (Psalms 119:69). It is to fabricate, from scratch, reproaches or lies.

4. Accumulation adds to invention: the word suggests a progressive construction, as one adds accusations or malicious thoughts one after another. The context of Job 14:17 (the transgressions "sealed in a bundle") reinforces this idea of accumulation.
H2950.origine: The Hebrew verb טָפַל (taphal) comes from a root that evokes the action of sticking, coating, layering. Its primary image is material and tactile: to cover with a sticky or plastic substance. The Segond translates it as "to imagine," which captures the nuance of invention or mental fabrication: just as one manufactures a thing by shaping it, one manufactures an accusation by inventing it from scratch. The word expresses an act of deceitful creation.
H2950.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, all in contexts of complaint or accusation. In Job 13:4, Job's friends "imagine" lies to accuse him. In Job 14:17, Job himself wonders if God "imagines" iniquities against him — the idea being that God would gather and invent grievances. In Psalm 119:69, the proud "imagine" falsehoods against the psalmist, while he remains faithful to the Law. In all cases, the word denotes the action of forging accusations or lies, often out of malice or pride.
H2950.portee: This word reminds the reader of the difference between truth and invented lies. The three passages highlight the danger of baseless accusations: Job's friends and the psalmist's enemies forge accusations that rest on nothing. True piety consists, like the psalmist, in keeping "with all his heart" the divine ordinances rather than being troubled by the lies imagined against oneself. It is an invitation to trust in God in the face of false accusations.

sens: High-ranking officer responsible for leading a military campaign or operation
Army or troop commander
H2951.detail: 1. The word refers to a high-ranking military officer responsible for organizing and directing war operations. In Jeremiah 51:27, it refers to establishing chiefs against Babylon: military leaders tasked with preparing the coordinated attack of several kingdoms. 2. It is also a chief or prince who commands an armed force. In Nahum 3:17, the princes of Nineveh are compared to locusts that suddenly disappear: they are numerous and visible, but also fleeting and insubstantial — an ironic image of their crumbling military authority.
H2951.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that denotes one who is at the head, who leads and organizes. It is related to other Hebrew words expressing authority and command. In biblical Hebrew, this term refers to functions of military and civil administration, often among Israel's enemies.
H2951.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in contexts of foreign military threat. In Jeremiah 51, it describes the officers that allied nations will establish against Babylon, announcing the punishment of the great empire. In Nahum 3, the leaders of Nineveh are ridiculed as fragile and fleeting locusts, contrasting with their impressive appearance. Both uses employ this word to describe military authorities that are enemies of Israel.
H2951.portee: This term reminds us that all earthly power, even that which appears powerful and organized, remains fragile and subject to God's judgment. The comparison of the Ninevite leaders to locusts invites us to place our trust not in human military forces, but in the divine sovereignty that overturns empires.

sens: To walk by taking small and quick steps
To advance in an affected or mincing manner
H2952.detail:
1. This verb describes the action of walking by taking small, quick, and short steps. It is the natural movement of someone who is hurrying or walking lightly. In Isaiah 3:16, the daughters of Zion walk this way "making the sound of their ankle bracelets" — a detail that shows it is not just about going fast, but doing so deliberately to be noticed.
2. The context of Isaiah also reveals a moral nuance: these elegant small steps mask pride and vanity. It is an affected and mincing gait, that of one who seeks to please and seduce through gestures rather than substance. The prophet denounces this coquetry as a symptom of a spirit of arrogance.
H2952.origine: The verb comes from a root that evokes short and quick movement, the idea of hopping or trotting. It paints the image of one who moves by small successive leaps rather than by long strides. It is a rare word in biblical Hebrew, creating a very concrete living picture.
H2952.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 3:16. It is part of a series of reproaches by the prophet against the proud women of Jerusalem, alongside other criticisms regarding their haughty demeanor, impudent looks, and flashy adornments. The prophet thus seizes on physical detail to reveal a state of the heart.
H2952.portee: This word reminds us that God sees beyond outward appearance — even in our gestures and gait. It invites us to examine our motivations: are we walking to go somewhere, or to be seen? Does our presentation reflect a humble heart or a spirit of pride disguised as elegance?

sens: Hard and horny part that covers the tips of fingers and toes in humans
Sharp claw or talon of an animal
H2953.detail:
1. The nail is the hard, whitish, and curved part that protects the tips of our fingers and toes. In Daniel 4:33, Nebuchadnezzar, having gone mad and cast among the animals, sees his nails grow like those of birds — a striking image of his humiliation and distance from his human condition.
2. The same word also designates the sharp claws or talons of beasts. In Daniel 7:19, the terrifying fourth beast in the vision has nails of bronze: an image of destructive strength and ferocity, highlighting the fearsome power of this regime that devours and crushes everything in its path.
H2953.origine: This Aramaic word is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew word צִפֹּרֶן (tsipporen), which designates the human or animal nail. The root evokes something that covers or protects, like a scale or shell. The Hebrew word appears particularly to describe nails in contexts of transformation or animality.
H2953.emploi: This word appears twice in the Bible, both in Aramaic in the book of Daniel. In Daniel 4:33, it describes Nebuchadnezzar's nails becoming as long as those of a bird during his madness. In Daniel 7:19, it qualifies the bronze nails of the terrifying fourth beast. In both cases, the word signals a monstrous transformation or an animal and threatening character: the nail shifts from the delicacy of man to the ferocity of the beast.
H2953.portee: These images of growing nails or metallic nails remind the reader that man, given over to pride or power, loses his humanity and reason. The nail becomes a sign of spiritual fall or tyrannical domination. It is a call to recognize God's judgment and to seek wisdom and humility rather than arrogance.

sens: To have a thick and obtuse mind, incapable of understanding or feeling
To have become fat or glutted, in a spiritual sense, due to indifference
To lack sensitivity to the voice of God and His law
H2954.detail: 1. The word describes a thickness of heart and understanding: the heart becomes "fat like grease," as the Hebrew says, meaning closed, heavy, incapable of receiving or understanding. It is the image of grease that accumulates and hardens, blocking access. In Psalms 119:70, the psalmist observes that the heart of the foolish has become thus, thickened, closed to wisdom — while he finds joy in God's law. 2. Spiritual insensitivity is thus a progressive closing off: one becomes indifferent, no longer feels, no longer receives. It is a deafness of the heart, not a momentary ignorance, but a settled torpor. 3. The word stands in opposition to receptivity, to attentive listening to God: one who is "insensitive" cannot welcome the divine word or discern His will.
H2954.origine: The Hebrew verb טָפַשׁ (taphash) comes from a root that evokes thickness, clogging, or encrustation. The related noun טָפֵשׁ (tapesh) designates a fool — not due to a lack of native intelligence, but due to a progressive obtuseness of the heart. The image is that of grease accumulating, making one heavy, immobile, and incapable of reacting.
H2954.emploi: The verb appears only once in the preserved biblical text, in Psalms 119:70. The psalmist, in this long hymn to divine law, compares the heart of the wicked ("their heart") to grease — dense, closed, insensitive. This unique occurrence places the word in a context of strong contrast: the one who sings the law finds joy and depth in its meditation, while those whose hearts are "insensitive" remain prisoners of their spiritual closure. It is a diagnostic word — to say that indifference to God is not a mere distraction, but a fattening of the heart, a cultivated deafness.
H2954.portee: This word calls the Christian to spiritual vigilance: sensitivity to God's word, the ability to listen, is never definitive. It can dull through habit, sin, or indifference. Remaining "sensitive" to God requires active attention, guarding the heart, and regular return to His law. It is an exhortation not to allow spiritual indifference to thicken within us.

sens: Daughter of Solomon during the time of the united monarchy of Israel
H2955.detail: Thaphath is mentioned only once in the Bible as the daughter of King Solomon. She married Ben-Abinadab, governor of the region of Dor under her father's reign (1 Kings 4:11). Her name means "ornament," reflecting her status as a royal daughter.
H2955.origine: The name Thaphath comes from a Hebrew root meaning "ornament" or "embellishment." In the context of Solomon's royal court, it underscores the prestige of the family.
H2955.emploi: Thaphath is named only once in 1 Kings 4:11, in the list of governors and high officials of Solomon's kingdom. She appears there as the wife of Ben-Abinadab and illustrates how King Solomon consolidated his power through political marriages with powerful families. Her mention highlights the political importance of these dynastic alliances during the united monarchy.

sens: Conduit par lequel l'eau s'écoule du toit
Écoulement continu et incessant
Ce qui use et fatigue par sa persistance
H2956.detail:
1. A gutter is the conduit installed at the edge of a roof to collect and direct rainwater. It is a concrete and familiar image for anyone who has heard water dripping regularly during a downpour. In Proverbs 19:13, a woman's quarrels are compared to an "endless gutter."
2. The word also evokes the continuous nature of this flow: drop by drop, day after day, without stopping. This is what is conveyed by "continuous" in Proverbs 27:15, where a gutter that flows regularly during rain illustrates endless fatigue.
3. Finally, the gutter symbolizes what wears down through its incessant repetition. A single drop does not break a stone, but a thousand drops pierce it. Similarly, an isolated quarrel passes, but the endless quarrels of a contentious woman are a calamity for those who endure them — just like a leaking gutter slowly but surely ruins.
H2956.origine: The Hebrew verb טָרַד (tarad) literally means "to flow drop by drop" or "to run off." The image is of water flowing continuously: first concretely through a leaking roof (gutter), then figuratively for anything that persists relentlessly. In Aramaic, the related word טְרַד (terad) means "to chase" or "to drive away," suggesting an action that pushes away, that distances — like water flowing away from what it encounters.
H2956.emploi: The verb tarad appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in Proverbs to describe a ruinous domestic flaw. In Proverbs 19:13, a quarrelsome woman is an "endless gutter" for her husband — an inexhaustible source of torment. In Proverbs 27:15, the comparison becomes clearer: just as a gutter that flows "continuously" during rain (troubling, untimely, inevitable), so is a quarrelsome woman. The wise man uses this common image of his time twice to show how repetition destroys: not through violence or flash, but through daily wear.
H2956.portee: This biblical expression teaches an important truth about married life and relationships: it is not always the spectacular crises that destroy, but the slow wear of daily life. For the Christian, it invites cultivating peace and self-control in close relationships, especially in marriage. It also reminds that repeated small tensions can seriously damage a relationship — hence the biblical importance of resolving conflicts quickly and seeking reconciliation.

sens: Expulser quelqu'un de force d'un lieu ou d'une situation
Éloigner, mettre dehors sans possibilité de rester
Contraindre à fuir ou à s'enfuir
Privé de sa condition antérieure
H2957.detail:
1. To chase means to forcibly expel someone from a place where they were. In Daniel 4:25 and 4:32, God will chase Nebuchadnezzar from among men: the king will be torn from his court, his greatness, and thrown out like an animal.

2. The word evokes a violent and definitive action: one does not chase someone one wants to keep close. It is to remove with authority, without immediate option for return. Nebuchadnezzar will not only be chased, but will live among the beasts of the field (Daniel 4:33).

3. To chase carries the idea of deprivation of one's former condition. The powerful king loses his throne, his palace, his human dignity: he is stripped of all that defined him. It is a total reversal, a degradation imposed from the outside.
H2957.origine: The Aramaic word תְרַד (te.rad) comes from the root טָרַד (ta.rad in Hebrew, verb H2956), which literally means "to pursue" or "to chase." This root evokes the image of someone being expelled, pushed away, forced to leave. Aramaic and Hebrew share this same family of words, with the sense of forced movement and expulsion.
H2957.emploi: The verb תְרַד appears only four times in the Bible, all usages in the book of Daniel. It describes the punishment of Nebuchadnezzar: three times (Daniel 4:25, 4:32, 4:33), the oracle announces or reports that he will be "chased" from among men. A fourth time (Daniel 5:21), the text recounts retrospectively what happened to him. In each occurrence, the verb emphasizes the execution of divine judgment on this proud king: he is chased from his royalty, thrown out like a beast, reduced to eating the grass of the fields. The context reveals that this punishment is temporary ("seven times will pass"), intended to humble the king and teach him that God alone reigns over kingdoms.
H2957.portee: This word reminds us that God's judgment is real and executed. Nebuchadnezzar, despite all his earthly power, cannot resist the word of the Lord: he is chased from his throne like an animal. For the Christian reader, this account teaches that no human power, however great, can escape divine justice. It is also an invitation to humility: the glory of the world is fragile, and God alone is eternal.

sens: Imposer un poids, une charge à quelque chose ou quelqu'un
Accabler, peser sur
Causer de la fatigue ou du labeur
H2959.detail:
1. The verb primarily means to physically impose a weight or load on something. In Job 37:11, God "charges" the clouds with water vapor, meaning He fills them, overloads them with this substance that will become rain: it is an image of the material weight that rests on a thing.

2. By extension, the word evokes the idea of overloading, of placing a burden. This can apply to things (overloaded clouds) or to living beings: charging someone with a task, a responsibility, or a burden.

3. The term can also refer to the effort, the fatigue that results from a load: to be loaded means to be overwhelmed by the weight of work or suffering.
H2959.origine: The Hebrew verb טָרַח (tarach) comes from a root that expresses the idea of weight and burden. The form used here (Hiphil) intensifies the meaning: it means not just to be loaded, but to actively load, impose a weight. This root fits within the semantic field of Hebrew words that denote effort, labor, and what weighs down.
H2959.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the context of Elihu's speech in Job 37:11. There, it describes God's cosmic action on the clouds: He charges them with vapors that flow down as beneficial rains. This poetic context, at the heart of the description of divine power over nature, shows that the word is used to express a powerful action that weighs on a material reality. The uniqueness of this usage makes it all the more striking: the Bible reserves it for this major image of the Creator who loads creation with His rain.
H2959.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the power of God that acts upon all creation. To see God "charge" the clouds with rain is to recognize that nothing escapes His action and that even the most grandiose natural phenomena obey His will. For the believer, this reinforces trust in the One who masters all of nature.

sens: That which weighs heavily, materially or morally
A heavy responsibility that one must bear
An obligation that has become tiresome or unbearable
H2960.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to that which weighs on someone, like a physical burden. Moses uses it when speaking of the people's complaints: they are a burden too heavy for him to bear alone (Deuteronomy 1:12).
2. It then evokes a responsibility that is overwhelming, what weighs and tires. It is the weight of duty that rests on one's shoulders.
3. The word finally takes on a more emotional meaning: a burden becomes that which is repugnant, what one endures with impatience or disgust. God says through the prophet Isaiah that the religious festivals of the people are a burden to Him, so displeasing are they (Isaiah 1:14) — not in themselves, but because the people celebrate them insincerely.
H2960.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning 'to be difficult, to cause trouble.' It belongs to the same family as verbs expressing discomfort or embarrassment. Its basic image is that of something that weighs, that hinders, that is bothersome — a burden in the broad sense.
H2960.emploi: The word appears twice in biblical Hebrew, always in a context of weight or difficulty. In Moses, the burden is administrative and relational: it is the weight of governing a turbulent people. In Isaiah, it becomes spiritual and emotional: a burden is no longer just difficult, it is repulsive, unbearable to the one who endures it. The word thus applies to both concrete burdens and moral disgust.
H2960.portee: This word reminds us that God does not call us to bear crushing burdens alone — Moses humbly recognizes this. He also invites us to examine our worship and observances: are they a joyful service or a burden that has become empty? For the Christian, it is an invitation to ensure that their relationship with God remains alive and has not degenerated into mere obligation.

sens: Recently cooked, freshly picked, not dried or rotten
That has retained all its strength, vitality, original freshness
That is alive, active, painful (for a wound)
H2961.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to what has just been prepared or picked, as opposed to what has aged or dried. When Samson finds a fresh jawbone of a donkey (Judges 15:15), it is a bone recently detached, still moist and robust, retaining its ability to strike — unlike a dried bone that would break.
2. The word also expresses the idea of preserved vitality, that which has not lost its original strength. A fresh wound (Isaiah 1:6) is an open injury, still painful, that has not healed — it is in some way 'alive' because it remains active and painful, unlike an old scar.
3. In these usages, the word always contains the idea of something that functions fully: a weapon that truly kills, a wound that truly hurts.
H2961.origine: This Hebrew word belongs to a small family of words revolving around the idea of freshness and present vitality. The primary image is that of something that has just been separated from its context or cooked, and that retains within it the energy and effectiveness of the present moment. It is a relatively rare word in biblical Hebrew.
H2961.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, once as an adjective and once to describe the state of a wound. In the account of Samson (Judges 15:15), it emphasizes that the improvised weapon has all its deadly power — it has just been detached and has not lost its effectiveness. In the passage from Isaiah (1:6), where the prophet describes the disastrous state of Israel under judgment, the freshness of the wounds emphasizes the current and painful nature of divine punishment. In both cases, the word highlights the present reality and active power of what it qualifies.
H2961.portee: This word reminds us that what is fresh, immediate, and alive has a power and presence that what is old or resigned does not have. For Samson, it is the strength of the present moment that allows for victory. For Israel, it is the current pain of judgment that cries out for repentance. In our spiritual life, this invites us not to ignore what is vivid and present — whether it be God's call or the conviction He produces in us.

sens: Previously in time, before something occurs
Not yet, not at this moment, a state of non-existence or absence at the time of speaking
Before the occurrence of an event, in anticipation
Before someone does something, in temporal priority
H2962.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to what precedes in time: what happens first, what has already occurred, or what comes before something else. In Genesis 45:28, Jacob says he will see Joseph 'before I die' — this meeting must take place before that final moment.
2. It also expresses absence or non-existence at a given moment: 'had not yet sprouted' in Genesis 2:5 means that the grass did not exist at that stage of creation, it was not yet present. It is the idea of 'not yet.'
3. The word can introduce a condition or an event that must occur before another: 'before crossing it' (Joshua 3:1) sets a temporal limit — the crossing will take place afterward, once the current moment is completed.
4. It is used to emphasize that an action must be done or heard before another begins: 'before the messenger arrived' (2 Kings 6:32), Elisha is already speaking, he anticipates the arrival of the messenger.
H2962.origine: The Hebrew word טֶרֶם (terem) comes from a very ancient root meaning 'to stop, to hold back.' The basic idea is that of what is 'held back' or 'reserved,' hence that which has not yet come, not yet arrived. In Hebrew, the word has specialized to express priority in time and provisional non-existence. It appears mainly in poetry and in significant narrative texts.
H2962.emploi: The word טֶרֶם appears 49 times in the Old Testament, primarily in classical biblical Hebrew. It is frequently used in Genesis to express what does not yet exist (the grass, the rain) and what has not yet occurred (Jacob's death). The Psalms and the prophets use it to express future events or future states: 'before the sufferings came upon her' (Isaiah 66:7) or to speak of God's eternity, who exists 'before' all things (Psalms 90:2). In Proverbs, it serves to give temporal warnings: 'before I die' (Proverbs 30:7). The context is always a reflection on the succession of moments or on what is yet to come.
H2962.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on the order of time and the power of God, who sees and acts 'before' things are. For the Christian faith, it reminds us that God transcends time, that He knows the future, and that He calls believers to live in conscious and careful anticipation of what is to come. It also teaches the importance of acting in time, before it is too late.

sens: To rip apart, to violently pull away
To devour, to ravage (referring to a predatory animal)
To destroy, to annihilate (in a figurative sense)
To nourish, to provide (rare causative sense)
H2963.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to tear apart or rip something solid. When Jacob says of his son Benjamin, "he has surely been torn to pieces" (Genesis 44:28), he imagines that a fierce beast has shredded him. It is the violent and destructive action of tearing.
2. The word often describes what predatory animals do: the lion that "tears its prey" (Ezekiel 19:3), the wolves that "tear their prey" (Ezekiel 22:27). It is the gesture of the hunter who seizes and ravages its victim.
3. The Bible uses this verb figuratively to depict political or divine violence: God threatens to "tear" without help the one who forgets Him (Psalms 50:22), meaning to destroy him, to tear him apart like a wild beast.
4. Rarely, the word means "to provide, to nourish" in the sense of "to supply one's share" (causative form): this is a less common and more abstract usage.
H2963.origine: The root טָרַף (taraph) fundamentally means "to tear, to rip apart." It evokes the action of tearing, fragmenting violently. In biblical Hebrew, it often relates to beasts that tear their prey. The word appears in both Testaments with this primary image of destruction and ravaging.
H2963.emploi: The verb appears 22 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the prophetic books (Ezekiel, Hosea, Jeremiah). It primarily describes the actions of fierce beasts: the lion that tears (Psalms 7:3, Ezekiel 19:3-6), the wolf (Ezekiel 22:27). It also applies to divine vengeance or the threat of destruction: God "tears" the one who abandons Him (Psalms 50:22). With Benjamin and Joseph's garment (Genesis 37:33, 44:28), it denotes the supposed trace of a beast that has shredded its victim. Once, it means "to nourish" (Proverbs 30:8), a derived sense: providing food is like "tearing" a meal to distribute it.
H2963.portee: This word helps the reader gauge the violence of destruction — whether physical, political, or spiritual. When the Bible says that God or evil "tears," it uses a wild image to show how radical and merciless this punishment or attack is. It is a vocabulary that does not allow for relativization: to tear is to completely destroy. For the believer, it is a reminder that turning away from God exposes one to real and total destruction.

sens: What a carnivorous animal captures and devours
Food, sustenance
Booty or wealth taken by force
Kidnapper, one who abducts
Carnage, violent destruction
H2964.detail:
1. The prey is primarily the animal that a predator catches to eat: a lion roars over its prey (Isaiah 31:4), the lion cubs learn to tear it (Ezekiel 19:3). It is the concrete image of the hunter and his capture.

2. The word also simply designates food, daily sustenance: wild donkeys go out in the morning to seek their food in the desert (Job 24:5), and God feeds the lion cubs that cry out to Him (Psalms 104:21).

3. Figuratively, the prey becomes the booty that the powerful take from the weak — riches and precious things that corrupt prophets violently appropriate (Ezekiel 22:25).

4. The word can also refer to one who devours or seizes: the mountains of the ravishers (Psalms 76:5) who forcibly take what they covet.

5. Finally, it depicts carnage, violent destruction: Judah returns from the carnage, like a satisfied lion (Genesis 49:9).
H2964.origine: The Hebrew root means "to tear" or "to rip away." The word primarily evokes the image of the lion or predator that seizes its prey and tears it apart. The same root produces words for "to seize," "to violently tear away." It is a very concrete word, derived from the observation of nature and the dangers of the animal world in the ancient Near East.
H2964.emploi: The word appears 22 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly among the prophets (Ezekiel, Isaiah, Nahum, Amos) and in the Psalms and Job. It is used first in the literal sense: the prey of lions (Psalms 104:21, Ezekiel 19:3-6, Isaiah 5:29). But very often it becomes an image of oppression and moral evil: corrupt prophets tear souls as lions tear their prey (Ezekiel 22:25), the land is filled with carnage and plunder (Ezekiel 22:27, Nahum 3:1). The psalmist confesses that without God's protection, Israel would be delivered as prey to the teeth of the enemy (Psalms 124:6). The word thus paints vulnerability and danger, but also the assurance found when one trusts in God.
H2964.portee: This word reminds us of the reality of the world: there are predators, powerful ones who devour the weak, injustices that ravage. But it also shows us that the Lord is stronger than all the lions in the world (Isaiah 31:4) and that He can deliver us from those who seek to devour us. It is a call not to rely on our own strength, but on God's.

sens: That has been detached or picked by hand, without tools
That is fresh, recently picked or removed
Image of deprivation, of what is taken away or deprived
H2965.detail:
1. The word first describes what is physically removed with the hands or by tearing — like the olive leaf that the dove brings back to Noah (Genesis 8:11). This green leaf shows that the earth is beginning to sprout again after the flood.
2. The emphasis is on the fresh, recently taken character: it is not a leaf that has fallen long ago, but one that has been picked or torn just before. It is proof that life is returning.
3. Figuratively, in Ezekiel, the word evokes the action of tearing and removing: the eagle will tear out the roots and remove the fruits of the tree, depriving it of everything that supports and nourishes it (Ezekiel 17:9). It is the image of total deprivation.
H2965.origine: The Hebrew word טָרָף comes from a root that expresses the idea of tearing, ripping away, removing. This root belongs to the vocabulary of direct and violent action: it is to take something away from someone else or from a whole. It is close to the image of the prey that is seized and torn away.
H2965.emploi: The word appears twice in the Bible. In Genesis 8:11, it qualifies the leaf that the dove brings back: a freshly torn leaf, a living sign that the flood is receding and creation is being renewed. In Ezekiel 17:9, it describes the action of the first eagle that tears and removes — an act of dispossession. The context is prophetic: it announces the dismantling of a tree that represents a nation or power. In both cases, the word emphasizes both the physical action and the recent, immediate character of the tearing away.
H2965.portee: This word reminds the reader that the visible signs of God's intervention in history are often simple and concrete — a fresh leaf brings hope to Noah. It also shows that tearing away, removing, depriving is an act that changes everything: it is how God humbles and brings the powers of the world to nothing. It is a lesson on the fragility of empires before the Lord.

sens: Animal killed and torn apart by a wild beast
Flesh of such an animal, considered impure or inedible
Figuratively: loot or prey
H2966.detail:
1. This word primarily refers to an animal (sheep, goat, livestock) that has been attacked and torn by a fierce beast. Jacob tells Laban: "I did not bring you any torn animals" (Genesis 31:39), meaning he did not allow the animals to be devoured by desert predators. This is proof that the shepherd has well-kept the flock.
2. By extension, it refers to the flesh of this animal that is not consumable. The Law of Israel forbids eating it: "You shall not eat any torn flesh in the fields" (Exodus 22:31). Anyone who accidentally eats it must wash and becomes unclean until evening (Leviticus 17:15). It is contaminated food, rejected to the dogs.
3. Rarely, the word takes on a sense of prey or loot: when the prophet Nahum cries out against Nineveh, he speaks of the "den" of lions, meaning the place where the prey they have torn is piled up (Nahum 2:13).
H2966.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to tear, to rip apart." It is a graphic image: the animal is not simply dead; it bears the marks of violence and tearing. In biblical thought, what is torn loses its integrity; this is why the Law excludes it from consumption and worship. The same word can also refer to a place where torn prey accumulates.
H2966.emploi: This word appears 9 times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated in the purity laws of Leviticus and Exodus (6 occurrences). Jacob uses it to prove his faithfulness as a shepherd (Genesis 31:39; Exodus 22:13). The Law forbade eating it (Exodus 22:31; Leviticus 7:24; 17:15; 22:8): it was unclean meat, just like that of an animal that died of itself. The prophet Ezekiel refuses to eat it, not even fat (Ezekiel 4:14; 44:31), as it is a sign of total defilement. Nahum calls it a "den" to evoke the ferocity of Nineveh (Nahum 2:13).
H2966.portee: For Israel, the prohibition against eating a torn animal is much more than a sanitary rule. It expresses a worldview: only what is intact, without defect, can be offered to God or consumed by a consecrated people. An animal torn by violence carries within it the disorder of the wild nature. By refusing this food, the believer accepts discipline, separation from the unclean, and manifests his consecration to the Lord.

sens: Group of Assyrian colonists established in Samaria after the deportation of the Northern Kingdom
H2967.detail: 1. Tharpel refers to a group of Assyrian colonists that the king of Assyria settled in the cities of Samaria after the captivity of the Northern Kingdom of Israel (around 722 B.C.). These colonists came from various conquered regions and formed an administrative and political community in the territory that Israel had once occupied.
H2967.origine: The name "Tharpel" literally means "those of the fallen mountain" or "those of the wonderful mountain." It designates one of several Asian populations that Assyria relocated to colonize the territory of the former kingdom of Israel, a classic practice of the Assyrian empire to weaken conquered regions and consolidate its control. The exact identity of this group remains uncertain in history, but the Bible includes it among the adversaries of Israel's return.
H2967.emploi: Tharpel appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 4:9, in the list of colonists and authorities of Samaria who write to King Artaxerxes to oppose the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem after the exile. These colonists were representatives of the mixed populations that Assyria had established in Samaria, thus creating a region hostile to the Jews who were trying to return and rebuild their nation. Rehum and Shimshai, named alongside Tharpel, were among the main opponents of this reconstruction project.
H2967.portee: Tharpel represents how enemy political powers have always opposed God's plan for His people. The appearance of these colonists in correspondence with the Persian king shows that God's people had to face formidable adversaries during their return and restoration — a lesson on faithfulness in adversity and trust that only God can fulfill His promises despite the hostility of the world.

sens: Experience an intense and deep desire
Aspire to something eagerly
Pine away while waiting
H2968.detail:
1. To long for means to experience a desire that pierces the heart — not a fleeting wish, but a need that stirs you. In Psalms 119:131, the psalmist opens his mouth and longs: he burns with desire for God's commandments, like someone who is thirsty and awaits water. It is a movement of the soul towards what one loves.
2. This verb also translates deep aspiration, the ardent desire that pushes us forward. It is less about dreaming in silence than actively, intensely turning towards the object of our love. The psalmist does not say he thinks about the commandments; he says he is eager for them, that he desires them with all his soul.
3. To long for can also express the languor of a soul that waits: that of the prisoner longing for freedom, or of the believer awaiting the presence of God. It is an expectation filled with emotion.
H2968.origine: The Hebrew word יָאַב (yâ'av) paints a movement of the soul towards the object of desire. Its root likely evokes the idea of opening up, stretching the throat — like an animal opening its mouth to drink. The word thus expresses the image of a deep thirst, an appetite of the soul. In Hebrew, this verb belongs to the family of words that describe the aspirations of the heart.
H2968.emploi: The word יָאַב appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 119:131. It is in the context of a prayer of the psalmist who confesses his love for God's Law. As he opens his mouth and longs, he declares his eagerness for the commandments — not as an external legal obligation, but as a desire of the heart. It is a cry of the soul that longs for justice and God's will. This rare but intense verb shows that the desire for God is not a moral calculation, but a surge of love.
H2968.portee: This word reminds the reader that the relationship with God is not cold or obligatory: it can be fervent, desiring, passionate. The psalmist does not say "I must" or "I have to obey" — he says "I long for." It is a lesson for every believer: do we thirst for the Word of God like water in the desert? Or is our heart lukewarm, turned away? This verb invites us to rekindle the desire for good, the thirst for God.

sens: Belong to someone, rightfully theirs
Be appropriate, suitable for someone
H2969.detail:
1. The word expresses what belongs to someone, what is legitimately destined for them or what they are worthy of. In Jeremiah 10:7, fear is "due" to God: it rightfully belongs to Him, as He is the King of nations and none is like Him.
2. The meaning extends to the idea of appropriateness: something that "is due" to someone is that which suits their dignity, position, or character.
H2969.origine: The Hebrew verb יָאָה (ya.ah) comes from a root that expresses the idea of adaptation and appropriateness. It evokes what "fits" someone, what naturally suits them. It is a rare word in biblical Hebrew, belonging to the register of dignity and right.
H2969.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Old Testament, in Jeremiah 10:7. It is used to affirm that fear "is due" to God alone, meaning it rightfully belongs to Him and He is its only recipient. The context is a celebration of God's greatness and His incomparability among kings and nations.
H2969.portee: This word reminds the reader that certain things "rightfully belong" to God: fear, honor, obedience. It invites recognition that giving to God what is "due" to Him is not doing Him a favor, but rendering justice to His nature and sovereignty.

sens: Son of Jeremiah, a member of the Rechabite family
H2970G.detail: Jaazania is a character from the time of Jeremiah, belonging to the Rechabite family, a community known for its refusal to drink wine and cultivate the land. He is the son of Jeremiah (not the prophet, but a namesake) and Habazinia. The prophet Jeremiah summons him and his entire family to the Temple to test them by offering them wine to see if they adhere to their ancestors' commandments (Jeremiah 35:3). This is a symbolic act: while Judah rebels against God, the Rechabites remain faithful to their ancestral commitment.
H2970G.origine: The name Jaazania means "Jehovah hears" or "God listens." It is formed from two elements: the verbal root meaning "to hear" and the divine name Jah (an abbreviation of Jehovah). This type of theophoric name, bearing the name of God, was common in Israel and expressed the confidence that God listens and responds to prayer.
H2970G.emploi: Jaazania appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 35:3, where Jeremiah summons him and his family to test their faithfulness to the Rechabite rules. This passage shows the unwavering commitment of this family to uphold the commandments passed down by Jonadab, the founder of their community. Jaazania thus becomes an example of religious constancy in a time of general disobedience in Judah.
H2970G.portee: The story of Jaazania and his family illustrates how sincere fidelity to what one has received honors God, even in the darkest moments. It invites the reader to consider whether their own obedience to God is as firm and voluntary as that of the Rechabites, regardless of the pressures of the world around them.

sens: Son of Shaphan, one of the elders of Israel during the time of Ezekiel
H2970H.detail: 1. Jaazania is an important man in Judah during the time of the prophet Ezekiel. His father Shaphan was a prominent figure, and Jaazania himself held the title of "elder," meaning he was one of the respected advisors or leaders of Israel.
H2970H.origine: The Hebrew name literally means "God (Yah) has heard" or "Jehovah hears," reflecting a trust in the God of Israel and His listening. It is a typical theophoric name from ancient Israel, where a person's name often expressed a prayer or affirmation of faith toward the Lord.
H2970H.emploi: Jaazania appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel's vision in chapter 8. The prophet sees in a vision seventy elders of Israel, including Jaazania son of Shaphan, standing before idols in the Temple, each holding a censer. This scene symbolizes the unfaithfulness and idolatry of Israel's religious leaders, and Jaazania is specifically named as a representative of this spiritual corruption within the ruling class.
H2970H.portee: Jaazania's fate reminds readers that high social position and family heritage (his father Shaphan) do not protect one from sin. His presence among the idolatrous elders highlights how unfaithfulness is rooted at the very heart of Israel's leadership. For the believer, this is a call to vigilance: even those who bear pious names and hold respectable positions must remain faithful to God.

sens: Prince of Judah at the time of the Exile, son of Azzur
H2970I.detail: Jaazania is a leader of the people of Judah whom the prophet Ezekiel sees in vision at the eastern gate of the temple. He is presented as one of the princes who give poor counsel to the people and whom God judges for their wicked thoughts (Ezekiel 11:1-2). His name means "the Lord listens," which contrasts with his behavior: although the Lord listens to His people, this leader participates in the injustice that God condemns.
H2970I.origine: The name Jaazania comes from Hebrew and literally means "the Lord listens." It is composed of "Jah" (Yahweh) and a verb meaning "to hear." Several men bore this name during the Exile, including a son of Shaphan and a Rechabite, but the Jaazania in the provided contexts is particularly the son of Azzur.
H2970I.emploi: Jaazania appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 11:1. Ezekiel sees him in vision among twenty-five men at the temple gate. God commands the prophet to prophesy against him and his companions, for they give bad counsel to the people and think that disaster will not reach them (verses 2-3). This is an example of the corrupt leaders that Judah experienced before the Exile.
H2970I.portee: The mention of Jaazania reminds the reader that even leaders and princes are not above God's judgment when they commit injustice. It invites the search for true spiritual guides, those who truly listen to the voice of the Lord rather than follow their own hearts.

sens: Judahite military officer at the time of the fall of Jerusalem
Son of the Maacathite, one of the leaders of troops who submitted to Gedaliah
H2970J.detail:
1. Jaazania is a Judahite military leader who appears after the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar. He commanded troops and presented himself at Mizpah with other officers to meet Gedaliah, the governor whom the king of Babylon had just appointed over Judah (2 Kings 25:23; Jeremiah 40:8).
2. He is designated as "son of the Maacathite," indicating that he came from a specific region. Along with Ishmael, Johanan, and Seraiah, he represented the last organized military forces of the Kingdom of Judah during this crisis period.
H2970J.origine: The name Jaazania (or Jezania, a spelling variant) literally means "God listens" or "Yahweh listens," composed of the divine name and the Hebrew verb "to hear." It is a classic theophoric name in Israel, expressing confidence that God answers prayers. The same character may be referred to as Jaazania or Jezania depending on the biblical sources, reflecting the spelling variations of the Hebrew text.
