H2970J.emploi: Jaazania appears only twice in the Bible, in the parallel accounts of 2 Kings 25:23 and Jeremiah 40:8, always in connection with the fall of the Kingdom of Judah. This is a critical moment: the temple destroyed, most inhabitants exiled, and the last surviving Judeans regrouping around Gedaliah, a governor installed by Babylon. Jaazania figures as one of the few surviving military officers, showing that even after the political and religious catastrophe, some respected leaders attempted to maintain a semblance of order. His role was to assist Gedaliah in administering the ravaged territory.

sens: Descendant de Manassé qui conquit et colonisa des villes en Transjordanie
Les bourgs et villes qu'il contrôlait, appelés « bourgs de Jaïr »
H2971G.detail: 1. Jair is a military leader of the tribe of Manasseh who, during the conquest of Canaan, seized many small towns and villages in the region of Argob and Gilead (Numbers 32:41; Deuteronomy 3:14). These conquests allowed him to establish his authority over a vast territory in Transjordan. 2. The name "towns of Jair" refers to all the localities he conquered and controlled; this name persists in tradition and biblical geography long after his exploits (1 Kings 4:13 and 1 Chronicles 2:22 still mention it as an established administrative reality).
H2971G.origine: The name Jair means "he enlightens" or "he who gives light," formed from the Hebrew root אור (or, "light"). It is a theophoric name that expresses confidence in divine guidance. Jair is the son of Segub, who is himself the son of Hezron of the tribe of Manasseh.
H2971G.emploi: Jair appears four times in the Hebrew Bible. He is first presented as a leader of Manasseh who conquered the towns of Argob at the time of entering Canaan (Numbers 32:41 and Deuteronomy 3:14). These towns remain associated with his name in the territorial administration of Israel under the kings: traces of it can still be seen during Solomon's reign (1 Kings 4:13). The genealogies in 1 Chronicles 2:22 preserve the memory of him by specifying that he had twenty-three cities in Gilead. His conquests make him an important figure of the conquest period.

sens: Region or group of villages in Bashan, east of the Jordan
H2971H.detail: 1. Jaïr designates a territory composed of sixty villages located in Bashan, a region east of the Jordan. In Joshua 13:30, this name appears as the name of this region with its many towns, distributed to the tribe of Manasseh during the division of the Promised Land.
H2971H.origine: The name Jaïr literally means "he enlightens" or "he shines" in Hebrew, from the root אור (or, "light"). It comes from the verb יאר, which carries the idea of shining or illuminating. It is not only a geographical name but also one that evokes a blessing or a beneficial presence over this region.
H2971H.emploi: The word appears only once in Joshua 13:30, in the context of the land distribution during the conquest of Canaan. This mention specifies that the region of Jaïr, with its sixty cities in Bashan, was assigned to Manasseh. Although rarely cited, this territory holds historical significance as a marker of the borders and territorial wealth promised to Israel.
H2971H.portee: Jaïr reminds us that God generously and precisely assigns the promised territory to His people. This name, with its luminous meaning, also evokes how God guides and blesses the settlement of His people in the Promised Land.

sens: Judge of Israel during the time of the Judges
Man from the tribe of Gad, established in Gilead
H2971I.detail:
1. Jaïr is a judge of Israel who governed the people for twenty-two years, a relatively long period compared to other judges. His name literally means "he enlightens," which may evoke the role of the judge as one who brings clarity and justice to the people.
2. He is from Gilead, a region east of the Jordan inhabited by the tribe of Gad. The biblical texts specifically designate him as "the Gileadite," highlighting his roots and anchorage in this border region of Israel.
H2971I.origine: The name Jaïr comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to enlighten" or "to shine." This name reflects a common biblical aspiration: that the judge brings the light of justice and wisdom to the people. Several characters bear this name in the Old Testament, but this one is distinguished by his role as a national judge and his long ministry.
H2971I.emploi: Jaïr is mentioned twice in the Book of Judges, in chapters 10:3 and 10:5. He appears in the list of judges who governed Israel after Deborah and before Jephthah, during a time when the people needed leaders to guide and protect them. The text specifies that he judged for twenty-two years, indicating a period of relative stability and peace under his authority. He is buried in Kamon, a city in Gilead, a place that marks his deep connection to this region.

sens: A Benjamite, father of the character Mordecai
H2971J.detail: Jaïr is a Jewish man mentioned only once in the Bible, in Esther 2:5. He is presented as the father of Mordecai, who becomes a central figure in the Book of Esther. Jaïr himself is described as a Benjamite (from the tribe of Benjamin), son of Shimei and grandson of Kish. Although his genealogy is given, the text recounts nothing of his personal life: he is known only through his familial relationship to Mordecai.
H2971J.origine: The name Jaïr means in Hebrew "he enlightens" or "he shines," formed from the root that speaks of light. It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries a divine dimension, suggesting that the one who bears it brings clarity or wisdom.
H2971J.emploi: Jaïr appears only once in the Scriptures, in Esther 2:5. He is named as the father of Mordecai in the genealogy presented at the beginning of the book. His sole mention occurs in the context of Susa, the Persian capital, during the return from exile. No act or word of Jaïr is reported; he is simply a genealogical link connecting Shimei to his son Mordecai, Esther's cousin.

sens: descendant of Jair
H2972.detail: 1. A Jaïrite is a man belonging to the lineage of Jair, an important figure of the people of Judah during the time of Egypt and the desert (mentioned in Numbers 32:41). It is a family name or clan designation: in 2 Samuel 20:26, Ira the Jaïrite was a state minister to King David, showing that he came from this recognized family line.
H2972.origine: The word "Jaïrite" comes from Jair (יָאִיר), a man of Judah from ancient times, and takes the usual form of descendant names in Hebrew with the suffix meaning "one who descends from." It is a patronymic, a name formed from an ancestor to designate all his descendants.
H2972.emploi: The term appears only once in the Bible: 2 Samuel 20:26 mentions Ira the Jaïrite as a trusted man and minister of King David. This unique usage shows that the Jaïrite was a respected family and that its members held important positions at the royal court, close to the king.

sens: to act without wisdom or discernment
to show a culpable or malicious folly
to lose reason or common sense
H2973.detail: 1. To act foolishly means to conduct oneself without wisdom or good judgment. In Numbers 12:11, Aaron acknowledges that Miriam and he acted "foolishly" by murmuring against Moses: it is an action devoid of reflection and fear of God. 2. This word also designates folly that is culpable and malicious, linked to the refusal to know or follow God. In Jeremiah 5:4, the little ones "act foolishly because they do not know the way of the Lord": this is not mere stupidity, but the willful refusal to learn and obey. 3. Finally, it is a consternation or loss of strength and common sense in the face of judgment. In Jeremiah 50:36, the sword strikes the false prophets so that "they may be like fools," meaning terrified and unable to react.
H2973.origine: The root of this verb evokes wandering, foolishness, and loss of sense. In Hebrew, the fool is one who strays from the right path, who refuses wisdom and the command of God. The word belongs to the realm of willful refusal and culpable folly, distinct from mere ignorance.
H2973.emploi: This verb appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the prophetic books. In Numbers 12:11, Aaron uses it to confess a minor fault. Jeremiah uses it twice to describe the behavior of the little ones who reject the knowledge of God (5:4) and to evoke the terror that will seize the false prophets (50:36). The word always emphasizes a moral responsibility: the fool does not act out of weakness, but out of a refusal to seek wisdom or through willful wandering.
H2973.portee: This word invites the reader to measure the gravity of spiritual wandering. The fool is not excused by ignorance: God reproaches him for not seeking His way and His law. For the Christian, it is a call to cultivate wisdom by listening to God and rejecting false paths, rather than being blinded by refusal or pride.

sens: To be willing to do something, to accept
To give one's consent, to acquiesce
To decide to undertake an action
To be resolved, firmly determined
To take pleasure in, to find it good to do
H2974.detail:
1. "To be willing to do something, to accept": this means consenting to a request or an invitation, showing that one is ready to act. Abraham says to God: "I have dared to speak," meaning "I had the audacity, the willingness to speak" (Genesis 18:27). It is the act of removing the internal obstacle that held one back.

2. "To give one's consent, to acquiesce": to respond yes where one could have said no. When one of the servants says to Elisha, "Please come with your servants" (2 Kings 6:3), he is asking for a clear agreement.

3. "To decide to undertake an action": to move from hesitation to resolution. Moses "decided to stay with that man" (Exodus 2:21): he consciously chose to remain.

4. "To be resolved, firmly determined": to have made an irrevocable decision. The Lord "has resolved to make you His people" (1 Samuel 12:22): it is an unshakable will.

5. "To take pleasure in, to find it good to do": to act because one truly desires to. David prays: "Now therefore, may it please You to bless the house of Your servant" (2 Samuel 7:29), calling on God to act according to His good will.
H2974.origine: The Hebrew verb יָאַל comes from a root that evokes the idea of being willing, of beginning to move. It is related to notions of beginning and active will. The form used in the Bible is the hiphil (causative action), which reinforces the idea of a deliberate will. The word expresses less a passive desire than a decision made, an act of the will that commits.
H2974.emploi: This verb appears 19 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books (Genesis, Exodus, Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings) and more rarely in the poetic books. It describes acts of human consent (Moses agrees to stay, a servant accepts an invitation) and divine resolutions (God resolves to make Israel His people). Its meaning oscillates between modest acceptance and powerful determination depending on the subject: in man, it is accepting despite doubt or hesitation; in God, it is deciding with authority. Some uses (Joshua 7:7, Job 6:9) turn it towards the past with the meaning "could have" or "would have liked," expressing regret about what should have been.
H2974.portee: This word teaches us that will is not an abstraction: it is an act that engages the whole person. For the believer, it reminds us that God is not indifferent, but actively chooses to bless us and make us His people. Conversely, we are called to exercise our own will sincerely, to say yes or no knowingly, like Abraham daring to speak before God or Moses accepting a new life.

sens: The great river of Egypt
Figuratively: that which rises and overflows
Figuratively: that which stirs and transforms
Figuratively: source of life and wealth
H2975G.detail:
1. The Nile is the great river of Egypt, upon which all life in the country depends: Pharaoh dreams of cows coming up from the Nile (Genesis 41:1-3), Moses turns its waters into blood (Exodus 7:15-21), and Pharaoh orders the drowning of the Hebrew male children in the Nile (Exodus 1:22).
2. The Nile also symbolizes that which rises and overflows: the prophet Jeremiah describes Egypt as "advancing like the Nile, whose waters are agitated like the torrents" (Jeremiah 46:7-8), an image of overwhelming power.
3. The Nile also represents a force that stirs and upheaves: Amos prophesies that the whole earth will rise and fall "like the Nile" (Amos 9:5), a movement of cosmic magnitude.
4. Finally, the Nile is a source of life and fertility for Egypt: Isaiah speaks of its banks where rushes and crops grow (Isaiah 19:6-8), and Nahum emphasizes that Thebes thrived on the riches of the Nile (Nahum 3:8).
H2975G.origine: The Hebrew word יְאֹר (yéor) specifically refers to the Nile and perennial great rivers. It comes from an ancient root that evokes the idea of flowing water and current. In the Greek Old Testament, this word is translated as "Neilos." The Nile was so central to Egyptian life that the Hebrew word came to symbolize the power of Egypt itself: when speaking of the Nile in motion, one speaks of Egypt acting.
H2975G.emploi: The word appears 36 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the accounts concerning Egypt and its plagues (Exodus 7-8), in Pharaoh's dreams (Genesis 41), and in the prophecies against Egypt (Jeremiah 46, Ezekiel 29-30). In the Exodus narratives, the Nile is the site of miracles: God transforms its waters, sends frogs and gnats, uses it to punish Pharaoh and protect the Hebrews. In the prophecies, the Nile becomes an image of Egyptian power: when the Nile rises, Egypt threatens; when God dries it up or troubles it, it is a sign of judgment against Egypt. The word also simply refers to the river itself in its geographical reality (Isaiah 19).
H2975G.portee: The Nile in the Bible reminds the reader that even the great powers of the world — Egypt with its majestic river — are under God's control. The plagues of Egypt, which strike the Nile, show that God commands nature at will to free His people. Understanding the Nile is to see how the Bible views Egypt: not as an invincible power, but as a land judged by the God of Israel.

sens: The great river of Egypt
Its canals and branches
Watercourses in general
H2975H.detail:
1. The Nile is the main river of Egypt, the one that traverses the entire country and makes it fertile. The Bible often refers to it when describing Egypt or the events that take place there. For example, in Ezekiel 29:4-5, God says to Pharaoh: "I will put hooks in your jaws... I will pull you out of your rivers," an image of the Nile in which Pharaoh reigns like a water monster.
2. The word also refers to the canals dug for irrigation, the secondary branches of the Nile that distributed water to the Egyptian fields. Isaiah 7:18 speaks of the "rivers of Egypt" where the Lord whistles for the flies, possibly evoking these canals as well as the river itself.
3. In a broader sense, the word can refer to any watercourse or drainage canal, as in Job 28:10 where it refers to wells or galleries dug in the mountain to mine minerals.
H2975H.origine: The Hebrew word יְאֹר (yeor) literally means "the Nile," as it is the river par excellence for Israel, neighboring Egypt. In Egyptian, the word y'r or iar referred to the Nile. The Hebrew root remains attached to this image of the great watercourse that brings life to an entire country. The word has also been applied to any canal or river, whether dug or natural, as long as they carry water abundantly.
H2975H.emploi: The word yeor appears 12 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in prophetic and wisdom texts. It is very common in Isaiah and Ezekiel, who describe the plagues of Egypt or judgments against Pharaoh: in Psalms 78:44, the Lord turns the rivers into blood during the plague of the Nile. In Daniel 12:5-7, a man clothed in linen stands "on the waters of the river," an image of a divine vision by a great watercourse. In Job 28:10, the word refers to mining galleries. Its use oscillates between the historical and real Nile and the poetic image of the divine river or the wonderful watercourse.
H2975H.portee: For the believer, the Nile reminds us of God's power over natural elements: He controls the rivers, transforms them, judges or saves through them. To see the Nile is also to recognize that God reigns over foreign powers and their resources. In Daniel, the river becomes the site of divine visions, inviting us to discern God's presence in the places of the history of nations.

sens: To abandon hope, lose courage
To declare something impossible or useless
To cease searching for or pursuing an effort
H2976.detail:
1. To abandon hope, lose courage: the word describes the inner state of one who capitulates in the face of a situation they deem hopeless. In 1 Samuel 27:1, David fears that Saul will not "renounce" his pursuit of him, meaning he will not cease his chase: David imagines that the king would lose hope of catching him.

2. To declare something impossible or useless: this means to assert that something is vain, that there is no point in pursuing it. In Jeremiah 2:25 and 18:12, the people say "it is in vain!", refusing to hear that repentance would be of any use: they renounce change in advance.

3. To cease searching for or pursuing an effort: to renounce also means to let go, to stop trying. In Ecclesiastes 2:20, the speaker gives his heart to "despair" after all his efforts, throwing up his hands in front of the absurdity of his work.
H2976.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of giving up, losing footing. It is related to the collapse of energy and confidence. The word expresses an inner movement: one who renounces lets go, they no longer struggle.
H2976.emploi: The verb appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the wisdom literature and historical narratives. It describes two main situations: first, renouncing the pursuit of someone or something (Saul who "renounces" seeking David in 1 Samuel 27:1); second, renouncing belief in the usefulness of an action (the people in Jeremiah who "renounce" repenting). Job describes himself as a "despairing one" (Job 6:26), showing the weight of one who has lost all hope. The context is always marked by a form of abandonment, whether temporary or profound.
H2976.portee: This word reminds the reader of the reality of human despair and its traps. To renounce before even trying is to close oneself off to the possibility that God can act. For the believer, it invites not to abandon hope, even in the face of obstacles, as it is a subtle temptation to refuse in advance what God can do.

sens: King of Judah who reigned for 31 years and restored the worship of the Lord
Son of Amon and Jedidah
Father of Jehoiakim, Joakim, Zedekiah, and Shallum
A Judean who returned from exile and participated in a symbolic coronation
H2977G.detail:
1. Josiah is the most significant king of Judah during the divided monarchy period. He ascended to the throne at eight years old (2 Kings 22:1) and reigned for 31 years. His reign is marked by a great religious reform: he undertook the restoration of the temple, discovered the Book of the Law, and celebrated a magnificent Passover in Jerusalem, the greatest since the days of the prophet Samuel (2 Chronicles 35:18). He destroyed the high places where incense was burned to false gods (1 Kings 13:2).

2. Josiah is the son of King Amon and Queen Jedidah (1 Chronicles 3:14). He embodies repentance and a return to God in the midst of a time of spiritual decay.

3. Josiah had four known sons: the eldest Johanan, Jehoiakim (also called Eliakim), Zedekiah, and Shallum (1 Chronicles 3:15). Jehoiakim became king after him and continued during the time of the prophet Jeremiah.

4. Another Josiah, a man returning from exile in Babylon, is mentioned in Zechariah during the time of the prophet Zechariah, in which case he participated in the symbolic coronation of the high priest Joshua.
H2977G.origine: The name Josiah means "the Lord heals" or "the Lord heals." It comes from a Hebrew root that denotes healing or relief. This prophetic name proved remarkably fitting since this king brought spiritual healing to the nation of Judah through his religious reform and return to the true worship of the Lord.
H2977G.emploi: Josiah is mentioned 47 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the books of Kings and Chronicles, as well as in the book of Jeremiah. He is first announced by the prophet a century before his birth (1 Kings 13:2), making him unique in the Old Testament. The majority of his references concern King Josiah who restored the temple and the Passover (2 Kings 22-23 and 2 Chronicles 34-35). His children are listed in 1 Chronicles 3:15, and Jeremiah lived during his reign and that of his son (Jeremiah 1:2-3). Another Josiah, a Judean returned from exile, appears in Zechariah at the time of restoration after the exile.
H2977G.portee: Josiah reminds the Christian reader that true religious reform begins with rediscovering the Word of God. Although King Josiah accomplished great things, his life also illustrates the limit of external change: lasting repentance requires a heart fully turned toward God. His story invites us not to neglect the passionate pursuit of biblical truth, even in times of spiritual decay.

sens: Man from the return of the exile, son of Zephaniah
House where the symbolic coronation of the high priest Joshua took place
H2977H.detail:
1. Josiah is a man living at the time of the return from exile after Babylon. He is the son of Zephaniah (Zechariah 6:10). The prophet Zechariah mentions him as the one where an important ceremony should take place: the symbolic coronation of the high priest Joshua.
2. The house of Josiah becomes the site of the solemn coronation of Joshua the high priest (Zechariah 6:10). This act symbolizes the restoration of the worship of God and the messianic hope after the return from exile. Although humble, this home becomes the setting for a major prophetic gesture in the history of the redeemed people.
H2977H.origine: The name Josiah means "Jehovah heals" in Hebrew (from the root that expresses healing). It is a theophoric name, meaning it incorporates the divine name, expressing the people's trust in the healing and restoration that God brings. This name is borne by a famous king of Judah long before the exile, but the Josiah of Zechariah is a man of the reconstruction period after Babylon.
H2977H.emploi: Josiah appears only once in the Bible, in Zechariah 6:10, in the account of the return from exile. It is at his house that the captives returning from Babylon come, and it is there that the symbolic ceremony of the coronation of the high priest Joshua takes place. This context shows that Josiah was a trustworthy man, worthy of hosting such an important act for the religious restoration of Judah. His role, though discreet, places him at the heart of the renewal of the people of Israel after the exile.
H2977H.portee: Josiah represents the simple believer who, without being a high priest or king, becomes an instrument of God's will. His house hosts a decisive moment in the redemption of Israel. This brief mention reminds us that restoration also comes through ordinary men who dedicate their homes and lives to divine worship and the community. It is an invitation to see greatness in the humility of service.

sens: Passage or opening through which one accesses a place
Access to the inside of a building or enclosure
Transitional space between two areas
H2978.detail:
1. The word designates the concrete passage or opening through which one enters somewhere. It is the point of crossing, the place where access begins. In Ezekiel 40:15, it refers to the space between the outer gate and the inner vestibule of the temple — this interval that must be crossed by the one who enters.
2. It can also refer to the access itself, the functional opening that allows entry into a building, courtyard, or sacred enclosure.
3. More broadly, it is a transitional space: neither completely outside nor completely inside, but this corridor of passage that connects two worlds.
H2978.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of going, walking, entering into movement. The entry is therefore the place where the movement of entry occurs — it is the place of passage. The word belongs to concrete and architectural vocabulary, particularly used in descriptions of the temple and its accesses.
H2978.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 40:15. It is in the grand vision where Ezekiel contemplates the very precise measurements of the future temple. The prophet meticulously describes each dimension, each door, each vestibule — and this word fits into this architectural description. The entry of the temple is not just a simple hole: it is a measured, ordered space, separating the profane world from the sacred world.
H2978.portee: This small presence of the word in a vision of a restored temple invites us to reflect on the notion of access to God. The temple has entries, passages, stages — there is not a single leap from the outside to the heart of the holy. This suggests that approaching God requires a journey, a respect for the established order, sacred spaces to be traversed respectfully.

sens: Man of the tribe of Levi, Levitical ancestor from the time of the Divided Monarchy
H2979.detail: Jeathraï is a Levite from the lineage of Gershon, mentioned in the genealogy of the temple singers. He is the son of Zerah and the father of Malchijah, and lived during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided between the Northern and Southern kingdoms (1 Chronicles 6:21).
H2979.origine: The name Jeathraï literally means "he whom the Lord leads" or "whom Jehovah guides." It comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of walking and divine direction. In the genealogies of the temple, this name reflects the belief that the Levites charged with worship were led by God Himself in their service.
H2979.emploi: Jeathraï appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 6:21, in a genealogical list of the Gershonite Levites. The same person is also mentioned under another name, Ethni, in 1 Chronicles 6:41. These genealogies document the succession of musicians and servants of the temple, establishing the heredity of Levitical service.

sens: To shout with a high or piercing voice
To express a strong emotion, a question, a complaint vocally
H2980.detail:
1. The word designates a cry that stands out, that comes forth with strength and clarity, often with a high or piercing tone. It is a cry that is noticeable, that resonates. In Judges 5:28, the mother of Sisera, looking through the window, cries out upon seeing his chariot delayed — she cries out in worry and impatience, and this cry expresses the urgency of her waiting.
2. More broadly, to cry out is to let a strong emotion burst forth through speech — fear, joy, anger, distress. It is less restrained than a simple statement: it is an exclamation that rises from the heart and cannot be contained.
H2980.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that imitates the sound of a cry — the initial "y" and the repetition of sounds already evoke this piercing vocalization. The form here (Piel) intensifies the meaning of the cry: it makes it stronger, more repeated, more expressive. This root is found in various contexts of lamentation or invocation in the Old Testament.
H2980.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible: in Judges 5:28. It is found in the Song of Deborah, where it vividly depicts the anxious impatience of Sisera's mother at the window. The verb captures a moment of raw emotion — this woman is watching for her son's return and, seeing the delay lengthen, cannot hold back her cry. This choice of vocabulary intensifies the dramatic contrast of the poem: while Sisera lies dead, his mother cries out waiting for him.
H2980.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not hide raw emotions. The cry of a worried mother, her impatience expressed without filter, reveals the humanity of biblical characters. It also teaches us that expressing one's feelings — fear, distress — before God and others is natural and legitimate; biblical faith does not require us to stifle our cries, but to direct them toward the One who listens.

sens: What the land produces naturally: the harvests
The income or benefit derived from the land
The absence or destruction of crops
H2981.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the harvests that a well-cultivated and well-watered land yields of itself: it is the wheat, barley, the fruits of the vine and the olive tree. In Leviticus 26:4, God promises Israel: "the land will yield its produce, and the trees of the field will bear their fruit" — the image is that of a generous land that unfolds in abundance.
2. The word can also mean the overall income or benefit that the land provides to the one who works it and inhabits it. This is why translators sometimes render the word as "income": the land is the means of living.
3. In contrast, the word is used negatively to speak of sterility: when God withdraws His blessing, "the land will no longer yield its produce" (Deuteronomy 11:17), or "the fields will not yield food" (Habakkuk 3:17) — the absence of produce becomes punishment and famine.
H2981.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to bear, to produce," the same one that gives "fruit." It expresses the idea of natural fertility: the land bears its harvests as a woman bears a child. It is a word familiar to the inhabitants of the Near East, where life entirely depends on what the soil gives.
H2981.emploi: The word appears 13 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the texts of the Law and the Psalms. It is often used in the context of divine blessing: the rains come in their season, the land produces generously (Leviticus 26:4; Psalms 67:7). But it also serves to express punishment: when Israel disobeys, God shuts the heavens and "the land will no longer yield its produce" (Deuteronomy 11:17; Habakkuk 3:17). The word finally appears to describe military destruction: the Midianites destroyed the "productions" of the land (Judges 6:4).
H2981.portee: This word reminds the reader that life, food, and wealth come from God and from the land He has given. It is He who commands the rains and the seasons; it is He who makes the fields prosper or dry up. The produce of the land is not an automatic acquisition, but a blessing that depends on obedience and which God can withdraw to correct His people. This invites the Christian to recognize his dependence on God and the gratuity of what he receives.

sens: Ancient name of Jerusalem
City inhabited by the Jebusites before its conquest by David
H2982.detail:
1. Jebus is the ancient name of the city of Jerusalem before David conquered it and made it his capital. The text of Judges 19:10 explicitly states: "Jebus, which is Jerusalem." This was the name of the city when it was still in the hands of the Jebusites, a Canaanite people who controlled this mountain fortress.
2. The Jebusites inhabited Jebus and fiercely defended it. When David approached with all Israel, the inhabitants shouted to him: "You shall not come in here" (1 Chronicles 11:5), but David took the fortress of Zion and made it the city of David, the capital of the united kingdom of Israel.
H2982.origine: The name Jebus literally means "threshing floor" or "place of threshing" — the image of a place where wheat is threshed to separate the grain from the chaff. It is an ancient Semitic name that likely designated the site before the Jebusites settled there. When the Israelites conquered the territory, Jebus became Jerusalem, a name that means "foundation of peace" or "city of peace."
H2982.emploi: The word "Jebus" appears only four times in the Bible, all in the Segond 1910, and only in two books: the book of Judges and the book of Chronicles. In Judges 19, a man and his concubine pass near Jebus (Jerusalem) late in the day; the servant suggests entering there for the night, as it is a Jebusite city. In 1 Chronicles 11, David conquers Jebus and takes the fortress of Zion, thus establishing his capital. These accounts mark the transition between the time when the city was in the hands of the Jebusites and when it became the heart of the kingdom of Israel.
H2982.portee: The name Jebus reminds the reader that Jerusalem, the quintessential holy city, did not always belong to Israel: it had to be conquered. It is a testimony to God's faithfulness who gave David and his people a fortified capital, the religious and political center of the kingdom. This conquest shows how God fulfills His promises and establishes His people in the land He had sworn to them.

sens: ancient Canaanite people inhabiting Jerusalem and its region
descendant of Jebus, the eponymous ancestor of this people
inhabitant of Jebus, the ancient name of Jerusalem
H2983G.detail:
1. The Jebusites are one of the Canaanite peoples that the Israelites encountered during the conquest of Canaan. Genesis 10:16 lists them among the descendants of Canaan, alongside the Amorites, Hittites, and other peoples. Exodus 33:2 and Joshua 9:1 mention them as obstacles to the taking of the promised land.
2. Their name literally means "descendants of Jebus," recalling their founding ancestor. They particularly occupied the mountainous region where Jerusalem would be built; Jebus is the ancient name of this city before its conquest by David.
3. In Jerusalem itself, the Jebusites resisted for a long time: Judges 1:21 reports that the Benjaminites did not drive them out, and "the Jebusites have lived to this day in Jerusalem with the sons of Benjamin." It was David who ultimately defeated them and established his capital on their land.
H2983G.origine: The name comes from Jebus, the eponymous Canaanite ancestor of the people. This place name, Jebus, originally designates the fortress and the region inhabited by the Jebusites on the mountainous site of what would become Jerusalem. The suffix -i indicates belonging to this group.
H2983G.emploi: The Jebusites appear 37 times in the Bible, mainly in the lists of peoples to be conquered in Canaan (Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy, Joshua). Deuteronomy 7:1 and Joshua 3:10 mention them among the seven nations that God promises to drive out. Their story is particularly illuminated in the historical books: Judges 1:21 shows their persistent presence in Jerusalem during the early days of the land distribution; 2 Samuel 5:6 and 1 Chronicles 11:4 recount how David ultimately takes their fortress. Individual Jebusites also appear: Aravna (2 Samuel 24:18) is one example. They thus symbolize the obstacle that the Israelites must overcome to possess the promised land, particularly the holy city.
H2983G.portee: The Jebusites remind the reader that the possession of the promised land is not automatic, but requires faith and obedience. Their presence in Jerusalem up to David's time also shows that God's plan unfolds gradually, not instantaneously. Finally, that David could deal with a Jebusite like Aravna with dignity suggests that even defeated peoples can find a place in God's plan when they submit to His will.

sens: people inhabiting ancient Jerusalem
descendant of Jebus, third son of Canaan
H2983H.detail:
1. The Jebusites are the people who occupied the site of Jerusalem before the Israelite conquest. Jerusalem was formerly called "Jebus" and was their main settlement (Joshua 15:8 and 18:28 explicitly mention that "Jebus, which is Jerusalem"). It was a naturally well-defended fortress in the mountains of Judah.
2. The name "Jebusite" comes from Jebus, the third son of Canaan according to the biblical genealogy. All the inhabitants of this territory around Jebus are designated as descendants of this eponymous ancestor, in the manner of other Canaanite peoples (Hittites, Amorites, etc.).
H2983H.origine: The Hebrew word יְבוּסִי (Jebusite) derives from Jebus, whose exact meaning is not entirely certain, but which designates ancient Jerusalem. It is a collective patronymic: just as we say "Ammonites" (descendants of Ammon) or "Moabites" (descendants of Moab), we say "Jebusites" for the descendants of Jebus. The suffix -ite functions in Hebrew as in French to form names of peoples.
H2983H.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, only in Joshua (15:8 and 18:28), during the land distribution among the tribes of Israel after the conquest of Canaan. Both times, it is used to clarify to readers that Jebus is none other than Jerusalem, the future capital of the united kingdom. This shows that Jerusalem was initially a Jebusite city before becoming Israelite. The mention of the Jebusite people then disappears, as after the city's conquest by David (reported in 2 Samuel 5), the Jebusites are no longer mentioned as a distinct group.
H2983H.portee: The term "Jebusite" reminds the reader that Jerusalem has not always been the holy city of God's people: it was first a Canaanite stronghold. Recognizing the former Jebusite dominance over the site highlights the miraculous nature of David's capture of the city and the establishment of the royal capital. It is also a geographical and historical anchor: the Canaanite context of the biblical world.

sens: Son of David, born in Jerusalem during the united monarchy of Israel
H2984.detail: Jibhar is one of the twelve sons of David born in Jerusalem, mentioned for the first time in 2 Samuel 5:15 amidst the list of children that David had in the capital. His name means "the Lord chooses," reflecting trust in divine providence. He also appears in 1 Chronicles 3:6 and 1 Chronicles 14:5 in similar enumerations of the royal lineage.
H2984.origine: The name Jibhar comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to choose" or "to elect," combined with the divine name. Its full meaning is "the Lord chooses," expressing the belief that this child was a divine choice. This type of theophoric name (containing the name of God) was common in the Davidic royal family to affirm divine blessing on the lineage.
H2984.emploi: Jibhar is mentioned three times in Scripture, only in the genealogical lists of David's sons: twice in 2 Samuel 5:15 and 1 Chronicles 14:5 with the same group of brothers, and once in 1 Chronicles 3:6 in a similar genealogical context. These brief mentions provide no detail about his personal life or his political or military role. He was the brother of Absalom, Adonijah, and Solomon, among other royal children.
H2984.portee: The name of Jibhar reminds us that even the children of kings, even those whose stories are only remembered by name, are included in God's plans and choices. For the reader, this suggests that every life, even those that go unnoticed in biblical accounts, has value and a place in the divine economy.

sens: king of Hazor who organized a coalition against Joshua
H2985G.detail: Jabin is a Canaanite king who reigns over the city of Hazor, one of the largest centers in northern Canaan. When he learns of Joshua's victories in the land, he gathers the princes of the north to form a military coalition aimed at stopping the Israelite advance (Joshua 11:1). His name means "he whom God observes," but what primarily defines him in history is his attempt to resist the establishment of Israel in Canaan.
H2985G.origine: The name Jabin literally means "he whom God observes" or "whom God contemplates." This king bears a theophoric name, meaning a name that contains a reference to God (God sees, watches over), but this did not prevent his revolt against Israel. His story takes place during the conquest of Canaan under Joshua, at the beginning of the establishment of the people of Israel in the Promised Land.
H2985G.emploi: Jabin appears in Joshua 11:1 as king of Hazor, a powerful city in northern Canaan. Upon hearing of Joshua's conquests in the south and center of the territory, he takes the initiative to gather the other Canaanite kings of the north to form a great coalition against the Israelites. This is the only mention of this character in the context of the conquest: he represents the organized resistance of the northern cities against Joshua. The Bible names him only once at this specific moment but does not recount the outcome of the ensuing battle (that of the waters of Merom), which is mentioned later in the same chapter.
H2985G.portee: Jabin illustrates how the refusal to recognize God's work leads to defeat. Despite his power and political strategy, he stands against God's plan for Israel. His story teaches that neither military strength nor the coalition of the powerful can stop God's purpose when He acts on behalf of His people.

sens: King of Hazor who dominated northern Canaan before the Israelite conquest
Leader of a coalition of Canaanite princes against Joshua
Military adversary defeated by Barak and Deborah
H2985H.detail:
1. Jabin is a Canaanite king who reigns over the city of Hazor (Judges 4:2). He represents the political and military power of the city-states of northern Canaan before the arrival of Israel.
2. He organizes a vast coalition of the northern princes against Joshua, mobilizing chariots and warriors to resist the Israelite invasion. The waters of Merom become the site of his decisive military humiliation (Judges 4:7).
3. Later, another king bearing the same name also reigns at Hazor; his general Sisera is defeated by Barak at the torrent of Kishon under the leadership of the prophetess Deborah. Israel's victory gradually asserts itself until the extermination of this Jabin (Judges 4:23-24).
H2985H.origine: The name means "he whom God observes" or "whom God considers." It is a royal Canaanite name borne by at least two kings of Hazor across different generations. The biblical context suggests that Hazor was a major regional capital in the northern Levant.
H2985H.emploi: Jabin appears seven times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the account of Judges 4, which recounts how God delivered Israel from his domination. One king Jabin (or his descendants) organized an armed coalition against Joshua during the conquest. Another Jabin later reigns; his general Sisera, defeated by Barak, seeks refuge with Jael (Judges 4:17). The final victory over Jabin is recalled as a liberating act of God in Psalms 83:10, where it is compared to the defeat of Midian. Each mention underscores the humiliation and gradual elimination of this Canaanite power.
H2985H.portee: The story of Jabin illustrates how God breaks the power of kingdoms that oppose His people. The victory over this warrior king, achieved not by brute force but by faith in God (Deborah the prophetess, obedient Barak), teaches that the Lord has mastery over history and that no earthly king can resist His plan. It is a reminder that true strength lies in God, not in wealth or military might.

sens: To transport, to carry physically from one place to another
To lead a person somewhere, to guide them
To bring, to present as an offering or tribute
To lead towards a destiny, an end (happy or unhappy)
H2986.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: to transport or carry something from one place to another, like carrying a burden. It is the movement of something going from here to there.
2. To lead a person, to take them from one point to another by guiding them. For example, "Who will lead me into the strong city?" (Psalms 60:11): this is asking someone to guide us there.
3. To bring offerings or gifts to God or to someone powerful. "Gifts will be brought to the Lord" (Isaiah 18:7): bringing the gifts to the temple, to the holy place.
4. To lead someone towards a fate, an end: to lead to death, destruction, or salvation. The lamb "led to the slaughter" (Isaiah 53:7) is taken to its end without resistance.
H2986.origine: The verb יָבַל comes from a root that evokes movement, flow, like that of a stream that flows. In Hebrew, this image of flow, of current that carries, unites all the meanings of the word. The same root exists in Aramaic (יְבַל) with the meaning of "to carry" or "to bring." The word evokes the idea of letting go, of carrying something with oneself in a continuous movement.
H2986.emploi: This verb appears 18 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the Psalms and in the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Hosea). It is used for very varied actions: leading people (a shepherd leading his sheep, a leader leading his soldiers), bringing offerings or tributes, and also leading towards misfortune or death. Thus, the wicked "escapes" (Job 21:30) the day of wrath: he is not led to punishment. Elsewhere, the maidens are "brought" to the king (Psalms 45:15). The context's imagery changes the meaning, but the heart of the word remains the same: something or someone is put in motion, carried, guided.
H2986.portee: This word speaks to us about the direction of our lives. We do not walk alone: we are all "led" by someone or something. For the believer, it is God who leads; for the wicked, it is their path that carries them towards judgment. The image of the lamb led to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7) evokes silent obedience and surrender in the hands of a greater power — a figure of the suffering Christ that speaks to us of sacrifice and trust.

sens: Physically moving something from one place to another
Carrying with oneself during a journey
Conveying an item from one person or place to another
H2987.detail:
1. This verb expresses the action of physically moving an object from one place to another. In Ezra 5:14 and 6:5, it refers to the precious utensils of God's temple: King Nebuchadnezzar "transported" them from Jerusalem to Babylon, and then King Cyrus has them "transported" back to Jerusalem. It is a concrete movement, involving a journey.
2. The word can also mean "to carry with oneself" during a journey. In Ezra 7:15, Ezra must "carry" the silver and gold offered to the God of Israel: this involves conveying this treasure to Jerusalem while holding or keeping it during the trip.
3. More broadly, it denotes the conveyance of an item from a source to a destination — not just the act of lifting it, but the entire process of getting it to its destination.
H2987.origine: This Aramaic verb (ye.val) is the intensive form of the Hebrew verb יָבַל (ya.val, no. H2986), which means "to lead" or "to bring." The root evokes the idea of putting something or someone in motion and directing it toward a goal. In the Aramaic of the Book of Ezra, this intensive form emphasizes the idea of effective transport, with all the efforts that this entails.
H2987.emploi: This verb appears only three times in the Bible, exclusively in Aramaic in the Book of Ezra, one of the rare Aramaic sections of the Hebrew New Testament. All three instances concern the transport of the temple treasures: first, their removal from Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar (Ezra 5:14), then their return ordered by Cyrus (Ezra 6:5), and finally the conveyance of new offerings for the temple by Ezra (Ezra 7:15). The historical context is that of the restoration of the temple after the exile in Babylon.
H2987.portee: This word reminds believers of God's faithfulness to His people: even in exile, the treasures of the temple are not lost, and God moves the hearts of pagan kings to ensure these goods return to His house. It also illustrates how God entrusts His servants with the responsibility of conveying His goods and offerings — a responsibility that is both concrete and spiritual.

sens: A flowing body of water
A stream or a small river
Water that irrigates and nourishes the land
H2988.detail:
1. The word refers to a natural body of water that flows — a current, a stream, or a small river. It is moving water, not stagnant water. In Isaiah 30:25, the "streams of water" burst forth on the mountains, imagery of abundance and fertility.
2. It can also specifically refer to a stream or a small body of water that winds through the landscape. In Isaiah 44:4, people "will sprout like willows near the streams of water," a comparison that evokes life, growth, and prosperity near living water.
3. The word is used to describe water in its role of irrigation — that which nourishes plants and land. The biblical image thus connects the physical idea of a watercourse with its life-giving effect: wherever water flows, life flourishes.
H2988.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to carry" or "to lead," which aptly describes the function of the current: it carries water from one place to another. It is a concrete word, linked to the observation of nature in the ancient Near East, where watercourses are precious and major landmarks of the landscape.
H2988.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both times in the prophet Isaiah, in oracles of restoration and blessing. In Isaiah 30:25, on the day of divine judgment, the mountains and hills will be filled with "streams of water" — an image of transformation and new abundance. In Isaiah 44:4, the people prosper "like willows near the streams of water" — a symbol of healthy growth and rooted life. In both cases, the watercourse represents a divine blessing, a mark of fertility and renewal.
H2988.portee: For the Christian reader, these images of streams of water remind us that spiritual renewal and true life come from God alone. Just as a parched land needs water, the soul needs the life-giving presence of God. These two passages from Isaiah promise that those who follow the Lord will experience this abundance — not the barrenness of sin, but the fruitfulness of a life nourished by grace.

sens: Antediluvian man, son of Lamech and Ada
Ancestor of nomadic herdsmen and livestock keepers
H2989.detail: Jabal is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, at the beginning of human history before the Flood. He is the son of Lamech and Ada, and the brother of Jubal, Tubal-Cain, and Naamah. His name literally means "stream" in Hebrew, which evokes the connection with pastoral life and livestock raising. The Bible describes him as "the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock" (Genesis 4:20): this means he is the founder, the ancestor of the nomadic pastoral lifestyle, that of shepherds and herders who move with their flocks in search of water and pastures.
H2989.origine: The name Jabal comes from the Hebrew יָבָל (yaval), which literally means "stream" or "brook." This image of flowing water is significant for a man whose descendants are defined by life with livestock, as access to water is essential for nomadic herders. The name thus reveals a connection between Jabal's nature and his historical role: he embodies the link between water, pastoral life, and nomadic living under tents.
H2989.emploi: Jabal appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 4:20. He is part of the genealogy before the Flood, in the lineage of Cain through Lamech. This unique verse presents him as the founder of the nomadic pastoral lifestyle: he is "the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock." This biblical formulation does not mean that he biologically fathered all herders, but rather that he is the spiritual or original father of this cultural and economic practice. Along with his brothers Jubal (musician) and Tubal-Cain (blacksmith), Jabal represents the three great domains of antediluvian human civilization: herding, music, and metalworking.
H2989.portee: Jabal reminds us that human lifestyles — pastoralism, nomadic life, livestock raising — are not modern innovations, but very ancient practices present since the dawn of humanity. His story also teaches that God recognizes and blesses different human vocations: Jabal the herder, Jubal the musician, Tubal-Cain the metalworker are all important in God's plan. This invites Christians to see their own vocation, regardless of their field, as something of value in God's eyes.

sens: Purulent wound that oozes and worsens
Defect that renders an animal unclean for sacrifice
H2990.detail: 1. An ulcer is an open wound that becomes infected and suppurates, meaning it discharges pus. The Hebrew word yabbel precisely evokes what "flows" or "oozes" — the lesion is alive, infected, and unhealed. In Leviticus 22:22, the ulcer is listed among the serious defects that render an animal unfit for sacrifice: blind, crippled, mutilated, ulcerous, scabby, or diseased. 2. From a ritual standpoint, an animal with ulcers cannot be offered to the Lord, as this defect marks it as unclean. It is a matter of holiness: the sacrifice must be without blemish, whole, and healthy. The ulcer is not merely a temporary illness; it is a visible corruption that disqualifies the offering.
H2990.origine: The Hebrew word yabbel comes from a root meaning "to flow, to run." It primarily designates that which flows or oozes — a discharge. The ulcer is a wound from which pus flows, a suppurating lesion. This connection with the idea of flowing or contaminated discharge clarifies why it is a serious ritual defect: it is a visible and contagious decay of the body.
H2990.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Leviticus 22:22. It is included in the list of physical defects that prohibit the offering of an animal. Alongside blindness, amputation, or scab, the ulcer represents a deep corruption of the flesh. The context is strictly cultic: one can only offer to God what is perfect and intact.
H2990.portee: The requirement for an animal without an ulcer reminds us that worship directed to the living God demands truth and purity. Offering to God what is corrupted, sick, or defective would be an insult to His holiness. For the believer, this invites consideration of the quality of what he offers to God — not in rituals of livestock, but in the integrity of the heart and life.

sens: City of Manasseh in the territory of Issachar or Asher
H2991.detail: Jibleam is a fortified city that belonged to the tribe of Manasseh, although located at the borders of the territories of Issachar and Asher. It is listed among the cities of Canaan that the Israelites were to conquer during the taking of the land (Joshua 17:11), but it remained in the hands of the Canaanites who were not driven out (Judges 1:27). It is near Jibleam that King Ahaziah of Judah, pursued by Jehu, was mortally wounded before fleeing to Megiddo (2 Kings 9:27).
H2991.origine: The name Jibleam literally means "devouring of the people" in Hebrew, formed from the root "to devour" and the word "people." This name was common in Canaan for fortified cities; it likely reflects either a locality known for its strength or a significant event related to its history.
H2991.emploi: Jibleam is mentioned three times in the Bible, always in connection with Manasseh. First in the text allocating lands to the tribes (Joshua 17:11), where it is listed among the cities that Manasseh possessed. Then in the account of incomplete conquests (Judges 1:27), where it appears as one of the cities from which the Israelites were unable to drive out the Canaanite inhabitants. Finally, in the dramatic context of Jehu's coup (2 Kings 9:27), where it serves as a geographical landmark for Ahaziah's flight. These three usages testify to the strategic importance of the city in Israel's history.

H2992.fr: perform the duty of a brother-in-law
sens: Fulfill the duty of levirate: marry the widow of his deceased brother without children
Take as wife the woman of a deceased brother without an heir
Raise up the name of a deceased brother by producing offspring in his name
H2992.detail:
1. The levirate is an ancient Israelite institution: when a man dies without having had sons, his brother must marry his widow to ensure a descendant for the deceased and not allow his name to be extinguished. This is the fulfillment of a familial and social duty, expressed by the verb yābam. The key example is Judah giving the order to Onan: "Go to your brother's wife, take her, as a brother-in-law" (Genesis 38:8).
2. This obligation is codified in the Law of Moses: "When brothers dwell together, and one of them dies without leaving a son, the widow of the deceased shall not marry outside to a stranger, but her brother-in-law shall go to her, take her as wife, and marry her as brother-in-law" (Deuteronomy 25:5). It protects the widow and preserves the family inheritance.
3. If the brother refuses this duty, there is a procedure: the woman goes to the gate before the elders and publicly accuses him of not wanting to "raise up in Israel the name of his brother" (Deuteronomy 25:7). Refusal was a shame and could be punished by a symbolic act.
H2992.origine: The verb yābam comes from the root y-b-m which denotes the relationship of brother to brother in the context of marriage and succession. Its basic image is that of the fraternal bond that obliges and endures beyond death. It is a specifically legal and religious term from ancient Israelite culture, related to the respect for the continuity of the name and family line.
H2992.emploi: This verb appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the context of prescription or illustration of the levirate right. Twice in Deuteronomy (25:5 and 25:7), which establishes the law in general terms, and once in Genesis 38:8, which reports a concrete case prior to the written Law. The context is always judicial or normative: it is about defining who has the right or duty to act, and how. The refusal or fulfillment of this duty marks the character of the person and their faithfulness to family obligations.
H2992.portee: This word sheds light on an ancient institution that showed how Israel protected widows and preserved the names of the deceased. It is a sign of the seriousness with which the Hebrews regarded family obligations and inheritance, even beyond death. For the Christian reader, it is an example of the old Law that Jesus did not abolish but reinterpreted under the sign of love: the Gospel of Mark (12:18-27) takes up this subject to show that the Resurrection changes everything.

sens: The brother of the husband
One who marries the widow of his brother according to Israelite law
H2993.detail:
1. The brother-in-law is the brother of the husband — the term designates the kinship bond between a woman and her husband's brother. It is a simple family connection.
2. In Israelite law, the brother-in-law has a special responsibility: if his brother dies without having had sons, he must marry her to perpetuate the name and inheritance of the deceased. This special marriage is called levirate (from the Hebrew *yavam*, brother-in-law). In Deuteronomy 25:5, the law commands: "the brother-in-law shall go to her, take her as wife, and marry her as brother-in-law." This is an obligation that protects the widow and ensures that the name of the deceased does not disappear from Israel.
H2993.origine: The Hebrew word *yavam* comes from a root that evokes the idea of "to raise" or "to cause to arise" — for the brother-in-law who marries the widow "raises up a descendant" in the name of his deceased brother. The practice of levirate (marriage with the brother-in-law) was widespread in the ancient Near East and was codified in Israel to ensure family continuity and the protection of widows.
H2993.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in Deuteronomy 25:5-7, where it is included in the detailed exposition of the levirate law. Deuteronomy 25:5 presents it as an obligation: "her brother-in-law shall go to her." Deuteronomy 25:7 considers the case where the brother-in-law refuses: the widow can then denounce him to the elders of the city and publicly accuse him of his refusal. This law protects Israelite widows without sons by ensuring them support and offspring.
H2993.portee: This law reveals how Israel protected widows and maintained family and property ties. It shows that a woman without a protector was not left abandoned: the community and family had duties toward her. It is an example of the social justice that God required in Israel.

sens: The wife of a brother
The widow of a brother, particularly in the context of levirate marriage
H2994.detail:
1. Sister-in-law refers to the woman married to one's brother — the one who has entered the family through marriage. It is the bond of alliance created by the brother's marriage, as seen in Ruth 1:15 where Naomi calls Ruth the sister-in-law of Orpah: they are connected through the marriage of their husbands (who were brothers).
2. The term takes on a particular significance in the law of levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25), the custom that requires a brother of a deceased man to marry his widow in order to perpetuate the name of the deceased. The grieving sister-in-law can then claim this right before the elders, and if the brother refuses, she removes his sandal as a sign of public shame (Deuteronomy 25:7-9) — a serious act that marks his refusal of his familial duty.
H2994.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root "yabam" which literally means "brother-in-law" or "husband of the brother" — it is thus primarily from the brother's perspective that the sister-in-law is named. This root also designates the practice of levirate marriage itself: the duty of a deceased man's brother to take his widow. The word carries the idea of this obligation of alliance and familial continuity.
H2994.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, all in contexts of marriage and familial obligation. Two occurrences are found in Deuteronomy 25:7-9, where the law of levirate marriage is outlined: the brother must take his sister-in-law in marriage if he does not want to be dishonored before the elders. The third occurrence is in Ruth 1:15, where Naomi refers to Orpah as Ruth's sister-in-law: they shared the same widowhood after the death of their husbands (Naomi's sons). The word is thus closely linked to two situations: the brother's marriage and the obligation to uphold the name of the deceased.
H2994.portee: This notion of sister-in-law reveals the importance of the extended family in Israel and the responsibility each person has toward their relatives. Levirate marriage is not a whim, but a law that protects the childless widow by ensuring her a protector and an inheritance, and that preserves the name and lineage of the deceased. For the Christian reader, it serves as a reminder that familial solidarity and care for widows are at the heart of the Torah and the will of God.

sens: City of Judah near the sea
H2995G.detail: Jabneel is a city that marked the northern boundary of the territory of Judah, close to the Mediterranean coast. It was located in a mountainous region, between Ekron and the sea, and served as a landmark to delineate the borders of the land assigned to the tribe of Judah after the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 15:11).
H2995G.origine: The name literally means "God builds." It combines the Hebrew verb "to build" and the name of God. It was a fortified city in ancient times, also known as Jabneh, which later became an important center of Judaism after the destruction of the Temple.
H2995G.emploi: Jabneel appears only once in the biblical text, in Joshua 15:11, where it is mentioned as a landmark in the northern boundary of Judah. The Bible lists it among the cities that marked the territorial limits of God's people after their settlement in the promised land.

sens: City of Northern Galilee, in the territory of Naphtali
H2995H.detail: Jabneel is a city mentioned only once in the Bible, in the context of delineating the borders of the territory assigned to the tribe of Naphtali. It was located in Upper Galilee, in the north of the promised land, and served as an important geographical landmark: it marked a passage on the border route, between Zaanannim and Lakkum, toward the Jordan (Joshua 19:33).
H2995H.origine: The name Jabneel means "God builds" or "God constructs," composed of two Hebrew elements: "yav" (formed from the verb "to build") and "el" (God). It is a classic theophoric name in Israel, expressing God's action as founder or builder. Other cities bear the same name in the Bible (notably Jabneel in Judah, to the south), but this one is the northern city, in Naphtali.
H2995H.emploi: Jabneel appears only once in the Bible, during the description of the borders of the territory of Naphtali, after the conquest of Canaan. Joshua 19:33 lists it among the landmarks that delineate the tribal possessions. This brief mention shows the importance of this locality as a strategic and commercial site on the north-south route of the land.

sens: Philistine city of ancient Palestine
H2996.detail: Jabné is a city located in Philistine territory, in the coastal region of Canaan. It is mentioned in the Old Testament as one of the fortified cities that King Uzziah of Judah conquered during his military campaign against the Philistines: he "broke down the walls of Jabné" (2 Chronicles 26:6), demonstrating his power and territorial expansion.
H2996.origine: The name Jabné literally means "building of God" in Hebrew (yav.neh). It is the same place as Jabneel (יַבְנְאֵל), another name for the same city. This city was located on the coast, in the region once dominated by the Philistines before the kingdom of Judah asserted itself under the kings of the Davidic dynasty.
H2996.emploi: Jabné appears only once in the Bible translated into French (2 Chronicles 26:6). It is cited in the context of King Uzziah's military victories, who strengthened Judah's power by conquering several Philistine cities and fortifying them. It is a geographical landmark from the time of the kingdoms of Judah and Israel.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin living during the Exile and Return
H2997.detail: 1. Jibneja is a Benjamite mentioned only once in the Scriptures, in the context of the reconstitution of Israel after the Exile in Babylon. His name appears in a genealogy that lists the inhabitants who returned to Jerusalem and were established in their lands (1 Chronicles 9:8). He is the son of Jerocham and is part of the ancestors of an important Benjamite lineage for the renewal of the people.
H2997.origine: The name Jibneja comes from Hebrew and literally means "God builds" or "Jehovah builds" — composed of "jah" (God) and a root evoking construction. This name reflects trust in God's constructive action for His people, particularly appropriate for a child born or named during a period of restoration and reconstruction.
H2997.emploi: Jibneja is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 9:8. He appears in a genealogical list of the Benjamites who returned from captivity and were reestablished in Jerusalem. This brief but intentional mention in the genealogies shows that even lesser-known figures of the post-exilic reconstruction were recorded to preserve the continuity of God's people. This man participated in one of the most decisive periods in Israel's history: the return and reconstitution of the temple and community.

sens: Benjamite who returned from exile
H2998.detail: Jibnija is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, at the return from exile in Babylon. He is the father of Reuel, from whom a line of Benjamites descended who resettled in Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 9:8).
H2998.origine: His name literally means "the one whom the Lord will build" or "whom the Lord will establish." It comes from the root "to build, to construct" and the divine name "Yah" (the Lord). It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God — a common practice among the Hebrews to express a desire or divine promise.
H2998.emploi: Jibnija appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 9:8, where he is listed among the Benjamites who returned from captivity to dwell in Jerusalem. He is identified as the father of Reuel, who himself is the father of Meshullam. These genealogies of the return from exile show the importance of tracing the lineages of the families that rebuilt the community upon returning from Babylon.

sens: River that runs through the West Bank
Stream serving as a boundary between territories
Border between Israel and the Ammonites
H2999.detail:
1. The Jabbok is a river that flows through the lands of Gilead, in the West Bank. Its name literally means "to empty" or "to flow," describing its action as a stream that traverses the mountains. In Genesis 32:22, Jacob crosses the ford of the Jabbok at night with his two wives, his maidservants, and his children, a memorable passage preceding his encounter with God.
2. The Jabbok regularly serves as a natural demarcation line between different territories and peoples. According to Deuteronomy 3:16, this stream marks the boundary between the territory given to the tribes of Reuben and Gad and the land of the Ammonites. This function as a geographical limit also appears in Numbers 21:24, where the river delineates Israel's conquest.
3. For neighboring peoples, the Jabbok represents a major political boundary. In Judges 11:13, the king of the Ammonites reminds Jephthah that Israel had taken his land "from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan," showing how this river was recognized as a significant territorial limit.
H2999.origine: The name Jabbok comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to empty," "to flow," a simple yet fitting image for a stream that runs through the mountains of Gilead, pouring its waters toward the Jordan. This river is a fixed element of the geography of the ancient Near East, located between the Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea, and serves as a natural landmark in biblical texts describing borders and the movements of peoples.
H2999.emploi: The Jabbok appears seven times in the Bible, primarily in the historical and legislative books (Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges). It is first mentioned as the crossing point of Jacob during his flight from his brother Esau (Genesis 32:22), a key moment in his spiritual life. It then becomes a constant element in the descriptions of Israel's conquests and territorial divisions: it marks the boundary of the territories granted to the tribes of Reuben and Gad (Deuteronomy 3:16), the border of Amorite dominion (Joshua 12:2), and the limit that God had forbidden Israel concerning the Ammonite land (Deuteronomy 2:37). In Judges 11:13, the Ammonite king invokes it to claim his lost lands. Thus, this river functions both as a historical landmark and as a marker of divine promises and limits.
H2999.portee: The Jabbok reminds the reader that God establishes boundaries and limits—both physical and spiritual—that shape the history of His people. Jacob's passage at the Jabbok symbolizes a turning point: it is there that he encounters the Lord and receives his new name (Genesis 32). Geographically, this river marks the promised lands and delineates divine victories. For the Christian, this word invites us to see how God directs history, establishes just boundaries, and can transform our difficult passages into moments of grace.
